sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: Gustav II Adolf of Sweden fought Poland through the 1620s for land on the Baltic. After the Truce of Altmark in 1629 he landed near Stralsund on 6 July 1630. That summer the emperor's Catholic allies forced the dismissal of Wallenstein and the reduction of his army.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: The emperor and his allies refused concessions on the Edict of Restitution, which drove reluctant German Protestants towards Sweden, whose army grew with French and Dutch subsidies. The sack of Magdeburg in May 1631 had dashed Protestant hopes. On 15 September the Swedish army joined that of the Electorate of Saxony.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Gustavus wanted a victory that would persuade other Protestant states to join him. Tilly, who had just taken Leipzig, intended according to Rickard to wait for reinforcements, but his deputy Pappenheim pressed for battle.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The armies met on a plain near the village of Breitenfeld, north of Leipzig. The 1911 Britannica describes a low east–west ridge between Göbschelwitz and Breitenfeld, held by the imperialists, with the allies opposite beyond villages along the Loberbach stream.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Britannica gives 23,000 Swedes and 16,000 Saxons against Tilly's 35,000, and Swedish guns outnumbering imperial guns 51 to 27. The 1911 edition gives about 22,000 Swedes, 15,000 Saxons and at least 32,000 imperialists; Rickard gives 42,000 allies against 36,000. The Saxons were commanded by their elector with Arnim; Pappenheim and Fürstenberg led Tilly's cavalry wings.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Tilly drew up his infantry in large blocks with cavalry on the wings and artillery in front. Gustavus formed two lines with a reserve, mixing pikemen and musketeers in smaller units and attaching musketeers to his cavalry. The raw Saxon army, formed like Tilly's, stood separately on the Swedish left.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: An artillery exchange ran from noon to about 2 p.m. Pappenheim's cavalry then attacked the Swedish right and was driven off. The imperial right broke the Saxons, who fled the field. Tilly's infantry turned on the exposed Swedish left, which re-formed to meet it. About 5 p.m. Gustavus counterattacked, and imperial resistance ended at dusk.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Gustavus kept his lines apart from the Saxons and held a second line and reserve. When the Saxons fled, he used them to form a new left flank instead of retreating. His right wing then wheeled, captured Tilly's guns and turned them on the imperial infantry.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The Saxon collapse seemed to open the Swedish flank, but the Swedish formation could change front quickly while Tilly's large blocks could not. The loss of the imperial artillery to the counterattack turned a stalemate into a rout.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The imperial army fled at dusk, with Tilly badly wounded; Rickard credits Pappenheim's cavalry with covering the retreat. Many of the imperial troops who surrendered, mostly mercenaries, enlisted with the Swedes.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: It was the first major Protestant victory of the war. The Swedes overran much of central Germany and Bohemia over the winter of 1631–32 and occupied Bavaria the next summer. Gustavus was hailed as the Lion of the North and drew several Protestant states into alliance, before dying at Lützen in November 1632.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: A coalition army is only as strong as its least reliable part, but reserves and flexible formations can absorb the loss of a wing. Artillery placed forward can be captured and used against its owners.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Force figures vary by several thousand between sources. They also differ on the opening: Britannica says a Swedish outflanking move provoked Pappenheim's charge, while the 1911 edition and Rickard simply have Pappenheim open the fighting. Britannica's verdict that the battle proved linear tactics superior is an interpretation.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Britannica's battle article and its history of Europe give the narrative and context, the 1911 Britannica the fullest account of the deployments, and Rickard a concise summary. No contemporary account was read for this study.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: In the War of the Spanish Succession (1702–13) a Franco-Bavarian army threatened Vienna and the Austrian position in Germany. To prevent an Austrian collapse, the Duke of Marlborough marched an army from the Low Countries to the Danube, unnoticed by the French, and joined Prince Eugene of Savoy's Austrian army.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: England, Austria and the Dutch Republic were allied against Louis XIV, while the elector of Bavaria fought on the French side. Losing Vienna would have threatened the alliance itself. The Bavarian side is given by the Neue Deutsche Biographie's article on the elector, Max Emanuel: hoping still for a share of the Spanish inheritance, he allied with France in 1701 and 1702, sought a royal title and sovereign territory, and was told by Louis XIV to win them by conquest within the Empire. He seized the imperial city of Ulm in 1702 to open a link with France, invaded Tyrol in 1703 and was driven out by its militia, and even negotiated for a royal title from the Emperor as the price of changing sides, which Leopold I refused. For France, the alliance was meant to keep the fighting away from its own frontiers.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Marlborough and Eugene aimed to save Vienna by defeating the Franco-Bavarian army. Marshal Tallard, expecting them to stay on the defensive to protect Vienna, did not think their slightly smaller army would attack.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Blenheim (now Blindheim) lies on the Danube about 16 km south-west of Donauwörth, where the road to Ulm passes between hills and the marshy river valley. The French front ran along the Nebel stream, covered by the villages of Blenheim, Unterglau and Oberglau, with its left in the hills near Lutzingen.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Britannica gives about 52,000 British, Dutch and Austrian troops under Marlborough and Eugene against about 60,000 French and Bavarians. The French army was in two nearly independent parts: Tallard commanded the right, and Marshal Marsin and the elector the left, where, the Allgemeine Deutsche Biographie notes, the Bavarians formed the left wing. The elector had won on the same field before, beating an Austrian army at Höchstädt on 20 September 1703.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Tallard placed a large force of his best infantry in Blenheim and his cavalry on the wings. The junction between his army and Marsin's was held by cavalry with little infantry support. Marlborough faced Tallard, and Eugene faced Marsin and the elector.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: Marlborough and Eugene joined on 12 August and advanced next morning over broken ground cut by streams. The battle opened about 12:30 p.m. Lord Cutts made two failed assaults on Blenheim while Eugene kept Marsin engaged; the Allgemeine Deutsche Biographie writes that the elector beat off three attacks by Eugene's imperial troops and threw back the Brandenburgers. Marlborough then crossed the Nebel, his cavalry broke the French centre and wheeled against Tallard's wing, and the troops in Blenheim were surrounded.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: The allies chose to attack a larger army in a strong position. Cutts's attacks drew more French reserves into Blenheim than Tallard intended. Marlborough made his main effort against the weak centre, helped by a cavalry corps that Eugene lent him.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The allied cavalry broke through at the junction of the two French armies, separating Marsin from Tallard. With Tallard's infantry packed into Blenheim, his centre had too little to stop the attack.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Tallard was captured and his army almost destroyed, many of its men driven into the Danube. The infantry and dragoons trapped in Blenheim surrendered, while Marsin and the elector withdrew in the dusk. The Bavarian biography credits the elector's composure with keeping the retreat in tolerable order, gathering the scattered troops into a fighting force again and bringing them through the defiles of the Black Forest.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The battle saved Vienna, preserved the alliance and knocked Bavaria out of the war. Britannica calls it the first major defeat of a French army in over 50 years. It began a lasting partnership between Marlborough and Eugene, and Queen Anne rewarded Marlborough with the manor of Woodstock and funds for Blenheim Palace. For Bavaria, the House of Bavarian History records, the elector fled into exile in the Netherlands, the country was occupied by Austrian troops, many Bavarians died in an abortive uprising, and Max Emanuel recovered his electorate only in 1714; the Neue Deutsche Biographie adds that he was placed under the ban of the Empire in 1706.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Allied commanders who coordinated closely could defeat a larger army whose two halves fought almost separately. Attacks that pin an enemy's strongpoints can draw away the reserves needed elsewhere.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Figures differ: the 1911 Britannica calls the French only somewhat superior in numbers, and the battalions trapped in Blenheim are given as about 23 or 24. The National Army Museum lists Prussians in the alliance, while Britannica names British, Dutch and Austrian troops; the House of Bavarian History names troops from Britain, Holland, Denmark, Prussia, Hanover and Hesse. In German the battle is the (second) battle of Höchstädt. The Allgemeine Deutsche Biographie, written in 1885, says Marlborough's storming of Blindheim decided the defeat of the French centre, whereas Britannica describes the village holding out until it was surrounded and the decision falling in the centre beside it; the same article quotes a historian's praise of the elector's leadership in the retreat, an admiring judgement. Verdicts such as ending the illusion of French invincibility are judgments.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Britannica gives the main narrative and the 1911 edition the timings and deployments. The National Army Museum's page interprets John Wootton's painting, made about 40 years after the battle. The House of Bavarian History and the Neue Deutsche Biographie and Allgemeine Deutsche Biographie articles on Max Emanuel, in German, give the Bavarian side: the elector's aims, his part in the battle and the occupation of Bavaria. No contemporary account was read.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: John Burgoyne proposed, and the King and Cabinet approved, a plan for 1777: Burgoyne would march south from Canada and Sir William Howe north from New York to meet at Albany, while Barry St. Leger moved east along the Mohawk from Oswego.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Control of the Hudson–Champlain route would cut New England off from the other colonies. But Howe moved against Philadelphia instead. Maloy writes that Germain approved both Burgoyne's plan and Howe's and communicated them poorly, and the handbook says the order for Howe to cooperate was apparently never sent. Burgoyne himself, as he later told the House of Commons, understood his orders as precise: to force a junction with Howe.

refs.locator: The British Plan of 1777; Retreat and Surrender

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Burgoyne aimed to reach Albany. The Americans aimed to stop him at Bemis Heights, where their line blocked the river road south.

refs.locator: The Battle of Bennington; The American Line

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Bluffs, ravines and heavy forest covered the ground in 1777. The American line, designed by Thaddeus Kosciuszko, was anchored on the river bluffs and left only a narrow corridor along the river. The woods north of it hindered coordinated attacks and the use of artillery.

refs.locator: The American Line; Guide to the Park

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: The handbook gives Burgoyne about 9,400 men at the start, about half British and half German with several hundred Canadians, Loyalists and Native allies, but elsewhere about 8,500. Horatio Gates replaced Philip Schuyler on 19 August, and his army grew from about 3,000 to 9,000 at Bemis Heights, with Daniel Morgan's riflemen in Benedict Arnold's division.

refs.locator: The Burgoyne Campaign; Retreat of the Americans; The American Line

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Burgoyne crossed the Hudson at Saratoga on 13 September, cutting his communications with Canada. On 19 September he advanced in three columns: Simon Fraser on the right, Burgoyne in the centre and Friedrich Riedesel on the river road with the artillery and baggage.

refs.locator: The Battle of Bennington; The Battle of September 19

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: Burgoyne took Ticonderoga in early July, struck the American rear guard at Hubbardton and fought a sharp action at Fort Anne, but needed until 30 July to reach Fort Edward. In the west, St. Leger besieged Fort Stanwix and, after the fight at Oriskany, withdrew when his Native allies left him. A raid for supplies was defeated at Bennington on 16 August. On 19 September the British held the field at Freeman's Farm at heavy cost. On 7 October a British reconnaissance in force was defeated, and on 17 October Burgoyne surrendered.

refs.locator: The Burgoyne Campaign to Retreat and Surrender

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Schuyler slowed the British by felling trees across the roads and stripping the country. Burgoyne crossed the Hudson having, in his words, read his orders “for an hundredth time”; he argued that nothing could have justified him had he not advanced and tried a battle. On 19 September Gates accepted Arnold's argument for fighting in the woods and sent out Morgan, but held about 5,000 men back. Afterwards Burgoyne neither retreated nor attacked: Clinton had sent word of an attack on the Highlands below, and the woods hid the American position. On 7 October Burgoyne sent about 1,500 men to probe the American left, and Gates ordered Morgan, Poor and Learned to attack.

refs.locator: Retreat of the Americans; The Battle of September 19; The Battle of October 7

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The handbook judges that Riedesel's arrival late on 19 September saved the British line. On 7 October the capture of the Breymann Redoubt, which covered the right and rear of Burgoyne's camp, forced a general retreat; Burgoyne conceded that once Breymann was killed and the Americans had broken in there, the camp could no longer be held. Arnold was wounded in the leg in the assault.

refs.locator: The Battle of September 19; The Battle of October 7

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Burgoyne retreated to Saratoga, where an American force grown to about 20,000 surrounded him. With provisions nearly gone, he surrendered on 17 October under a convention that his troops would be shipped to England. Congress did not keep the terms, and the prisoners were held in America.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: News of the surrender reached France's foreign minister, Vergennes, in December 1777. Hearing of possible British peace offers, he decided not to wait for Spain, and on 6 February 1778 France signed treaties of alliance and of commerce with the United States. Maloy adds that French entry forced Britain to spread its forces across the world.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: A plan of converging columns failed when one column went elsewhere and another was turned back. An invading army far from its supplies, in country stripped before it, steadily weakened while its opponent grew.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The handbook, written in 1950, spreads the blame across Germain, Howe, Clinton, St. Leger and Burgoyne's lack of drive. It credits Arnold, Morgan and militia mobilisation, and says Fraser was perhaps shot by a marksman Morgan assigned. Its own figures for Burgoyne's army do not agree. Accounts of Arnold on 7 October differ: Burgoyne heard that he attacked without consulting Gates, while Maloy has him pressing a reluctant Gates for permission, after Gates had left him out of his report on the first battle. Burgoyne's narrative is a defence of his conduct before Parliament and argues that, had Clinton's attack come in time, he would have broken through.

refs.locator: The Battle of October 7; Retreat and Surrender

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: The main source is an older National Park Service handbook, read section by section. Burgoyne's State of the Expedition, his narrative and evidence laid before the House of Commons and published in 1780, gives the British commander's own reasoning; it was read in a scanned copy whose machine-read text is imperfect. Maloy's article for the American Battlefield Trust gives a modern account of the whole campaign. The Office of the Historian essay, from a series no longer maintained, covers the French alliance. No German or American participant accounts were read.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: After defeats at Mars-la-Tour and Gravelotte in August 1870, Marshal Bazaine's army was besieged in Metz. Marshal MacMahon's Army of Châlons was the only French army left in the field.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Britannica says Napoleon III, ill and in severe pain, could not fall back on Paris because such an admission of failure would doom his dynasty. The emperor accompanied the army but MacMahon held command. Moltke records that MacMahon first resolved to fall back on Paris against the wishes of the Empress and the ministry, turned east only on news that Bazaine might break out, and was overruled when he ordered a retreat on 27 August: the minister of war warned that if he left Bazaine in the lurch, revolution would break out.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: MacMahon advanced north towards the Belgian border, intending to turn south-east and relieve Metz. The Germans under Helmuth von Moltke knew of his intentions and moved to intercept him: Moltke writes that speeches in Paris and a telegram quoting Le Temps gave the march away, and that he had that day worked out a march table to wheel his armies to the right if it came.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Sedan was a small fortress town on the Meuse that could neither feed nor hold the army. Heights surrounded it, from Frénois, where King Wilhelm and Bismarck watched, to the Plateau d'Illy in the north; Bazeilles lay to the south-east. Moltke calls the height of Illy a very important point, since the road to neutral Belgium ran through it, and Bazeilles an exposed salient once the Meuse bridges were lost.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: About 120,000 French troops faced more than 200,000 Germans; the Fondation Napoléon gives nearly 600 French and 800 German guns. Two German armies, under the Crown Prince of Prussia and Prince Albert of Saxony, closed on the town.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: MacMahon's corps gathered around the citadel. Marine infantry held Bazeilles, and General Margueritte's reserve cavalry stood on the Plateau d'Illy.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: After clashes at Nouart, Beaumont and Bazeilles on 29–31 August, MacMahon fell back into Sedan. Early on 1 September, in thick mist, Bavarian troops attacked Bazeilles, where inhabitants joined the street fighting, and MacMahon was badly wounded. Command passed in confusion between Ducrot and Wimpffen while German armies closed the ring, nearly complete by ten o'clock in Moltke's account, and French cavalry charged in vain to break it.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: MacMahon named Ducrot his successor, passing over two senior corps commanders. Ducrot ordered a retreat westward towards Mézières. Wimpffen, claiming authority from the war minister, countermanded him and attacked towards Bazeilles to open a road east to Carignan; Moltke notes that Ducrot submitted without protest. In his own account Wimpffen writes that at half past eight he sent Ducrot a note saying the enemy was weakening on the right, that there was no question of retreat and that he held a letter from the minister naming him commander; his plan was to throw the Bavarians back into the Meuse and then turn the whole army on the Germans' other wing. Late in the day Napoleon refused to lead a final breakout, judging that it would only bring pointless slaughter, and ordered negotiations.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: MacMahon's wound left the army under three commanders in a few hours, with conflicting orders and few maps, while German artillery ringed the town. The Fondation Napoléon attributes the disaster largely to this breakdown in communication. Moltke judges that the exhausted French army could no longer manage a disciplined march under fire and could only fight where it stood. Wimpffen writes that the retreat Ducrot had begun made the 12th Corps give up the heights of Bazeilles and the 1st Corps the heights above Givonne, which could not be retaken, and that by mid-morning General Douay told him they were fighting only for the honour of their arms.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: A white flag was raised and Napoleon offered his sword to King Wilhelm, which the Germans treated as a personal surrender only. Moltke and Bismarck demanded unconditional surrender: in Moltke's account, the disarmament and captivity of the whole army, with officers free on parole, under threat of renewed bombardment. Wimpffen signed on 2 September. The army went into captivity and the emperor was held at Wilhelmshöhe.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: When the news reached Paris, a popular uprising overthrew the Second Empire, and the Republic was proclaimed on 4 September. The new government would not accept German terms, and the war went on for five more months.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: An operation driven by dynastic politics led an army into a place it could not supply or hold. A command that changed hands mid-battle could not carry out any single plan.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The two modern accounts disagree on the timing of the white flag: Britannica says early on 2 September, the Fondation Napoléon on the afternoon of 1 September, and Moltke puts the white flags on the towers at about half past four that afternoon. They name different breakout routes and describe the emperor's surrender differently. Their figures for prisoners also differ. Moltke, the victor's chief of staff, judges that Wimpffen was not to blame for the army's plight and that MacMahon was fortunate to be wounded before he had to sign. The two French generals published opposing books in 1871. Wimpffen argues that the road to Mézières was already blocked by German corps on the right bank, that a retreat by Illy would have been caught in the open and that escape into Belgium would have meant laying down arms without a fight; he accuses Ducrot of compromising the day. Ducrot, answering what he lists as Wimpffen's accusations, including desertion of the field and disobedience, argues that a retreat north by Illy towards Mézières would have reached supplies and reinforcements and kept contact with Paris, while a breakout east by Carignan would have run into the German army before Metz. Each book is a defence of its author, and their figures are not used.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Britannica's article and the Fondation Napoléon's account, which draws on French and German scholarship, are the modern sources read. Moltke's own history of the war, in the revised English translation of 1893, gives the German chief of staff's account of the march and the battle. The rival books of the French generals Wimpffen and Ducrot, both of 1871 and in French, on the Internet Archive, give the French command's own accounts of the dispute over retreat or breakout.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: Russia and Japan both sought dominance in Manchuria and Korea. On 8 February 1904 Admiral Tōgō Heihachirō's ships attacked the Russian squadron at Port Arthur before Japan's declaration of war, then blockaded the port. The able Russian commander, Admiral Makarov, was killed in April.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Japan had not secured complete command of the sea. In 1904 the tsar decided to send much of the Baltic Fleet, renamed the Second Pacific Squadron, to break the blockade; Okabe shows Japan learning of the plan by late May 1904 from reports that often contradicted each other about whether it would sail. Port Arthur fell on 2 January 1905, before it arrived.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: The squadron was first meant to join the Port Arthur squadron and overwhelm the Japanese navy; after Port Arthur fell, its aim became to reach Vladivostok. Tōgō aimed to intercept and destroy it.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The voyage covered about 18,000 miles with no Russian bases on the way, and French and Portuguese ports turned the squadron away. From Indochina it could reach Vladivostok by the Soya or Tsugaru straits or through the Tsushima Strait; Admiral Zinovy Rozhestvensky chose Tsushima, where Tōgō waited near Pusan on the Korean coast. Japan had covered the approaches with observation towers linked to headquarters by cable and wireless, including one on the island of Okinoshima.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Butler counts 38 Russian combatants, including 12 battleships, ranging from very old ships to the newest; many crews had little ocean-going experience. Britannica calls many of the ships old and unserviceable and the Japanese ships superior in speed and armament.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Before dawn on 27 May the auxiliary cruiser Shinano Maru sighted the Russian fleet and reported it by wireless, and the Combined Fleet sailed from Jinhae Bay, led by the Mikasa, to intercept it near Okinoshima. Japanese cruisers shadowed the Russians from early on 27 May. Rozhestvensky tried to form line abreast, but only three battleships managed it, so he reverted to two columns with his four newest battleships on the right.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: The squadron left the Baltic in October 1904 and fired on British trawlers off the Dogger Bank; Japanese diplomats and their informants followed it through Vigo, Madagascar and the bays of Indochina, from which its departure on 14 May was confirmed. At Nossi-Bé off Madagascar it learned that Port Arthur had fallen, and off Indochina it waited for reinforcements. On 27 May, in fog that a shrine log on Okinoshima says limited visibility to about five nautical miles, Tōgō's fleet crossed ahead of it and turned, and the leading Russian battleships were quickly disabled. Night torpedo attacks followed, and on 28 May Rear Admiral Nebogatov surrendered.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: After Nossi-Bé, Rozhestvensky proposed returning but went on, expecting reinforcements. He opened fire at 13:49 while the Japanese fleet was turning. Wounded, he was moved to a destroyer; Nebogatov led the remnant north-east, and Rear Admiral Enkvist took his cruisers south to Manila.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The Russian gunners missed during the Japanese turn, and Japanese fire soon disabled the leading battleships, including the flagship. With its commander wounded, the battle became a melee that the Russians could not control.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Most of the Russian fleet was sunk, captured or interned, and Rozhestvensky, wounded, was taken prisoner. Britannica says four ships reached Vladivostok; Butler says three of 38 combatants eventually did, and Okabe names them as the cruiser Almaz and two destroyers. Nebogatov surrendered the ships still with him.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Within a few hundred miles of its destination, the Baltic Fleet was shattered, and with it Russia's hope of regaining command of the sea. The war ended in disaster for imperial Russia.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: A fleet sent across the world without bases arrived worn down before it fought. Butler applies Clausewitz's idea of friction: heat, disease, spoiled food, lack of mail and leave, and exhausting coaling at sea all lowered readiness.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Butler argues that most analyses stress material weaknesses and underrate the human friction of the voyage and Rozhestvensky's leadership. The sources differ on details: the battle is dated 27–28 or 27–29 May, the Dogger Bank incident 21 October or the night of 22–23 October, and the ships reaching Vladivostok as three or four. Even the weather is reported differently: Kawano sets the Mikasa's telegram that the weather was fine but the waves high against the fog recorded on Okinoshima.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Butler draws on Russian participant memoirs and on Westwood, Hough and Pleshakov. Britannica gives a concise summary. The two Japan Center for Asian Historical Records articles draw on Japanese archives: Foreign Ministry telegrams on tracking the fleet, and the records of the observation network and a shrine log from Okinoshima. Butler places Vladivostok on Kamchatka, an error not followed here.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: Sinor dates the first episode of the Mongol western campaign to the taking of Bulghar on the Volga in the autumn of 1237. Ryazan fell on 21 December 1237, followed by Kolomna, Vladimir, Suzdal and Moscow, and Kiev fell on 6 December 1240 after a siege of nine days. With Kievan Rus' subjugated, Britannica writes, the Mongols turned to Hungary.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Béla IV, king of Hungary from 1235, had admitted the Cuman leader Koten and his people: Sinor has him receive Koten at the frontier on Easter Day 1239 and stand godfather at his baptism. After Mongol units had reached Pest, suspicion of Cuman treachery turned to violence: Koten and his entourage were killed by a mob, and his people left the kingdom in a mass exodus. Duke Frederick of Austria promised help against the Mongols, which Britannica says he never delivered, and seized western parts of the kingdom as its price.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Britannica credits Subutai with planning a three-pronged assault on Hungary supported by a campaign in Poland. Sinor treats the operation as one planned campaign carried out by separate corps, with Batu's main body entering Hungary from the north. Stephen Pow and József Laszlovszky, using both the European chronicles and the Asian sources, argue that a vanguard under Batu's brother Shiban went far ahead to provoke the Hungarian army near Pest and lure it to a site chosen in advance, while Batu and the main body stayed in north-eastern Hungary. The sources read do not say what the Mongol leaders intended beyond the defeat of Hungary.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Sinor places the contact a little less than halfway between Pest and the Verecke pass, near the river Sajó. The Mongols halted on one bank and Béla encamped on the other, so the battle turned on crossing the river; Britannica has Subutai ride north in search of a ford. Recent research on the battlefield, Pow and Laszlovszky report, has located the medieval village of Hídvég, “end of the bridge”, away from the present-day village of the name, and shown that the confluence of the Sajó and the Hernád then lay elsewhere; the Chinese–Mongolian biography of Sübe'etei names the river of the battle as one that was probably the Hernád. Gallery forest along the river could hide the Mongols' movements, and no hills stand near the battlefield today.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Sinor sets out the Mongol command: on the right, facing west, Batu's brother Orda, seconded by Baidar and Qaidan, sons of Chagadai; Batu in the centre, seconded by Subetei and Shiban; and a corps under Qadan, son of the Great Khan Ögedei, assisted by Bori, a grandson of Chagadai. Command was shared among princes of the ruling house, with Subutai as the senior general. Béla commanded the Hungarian army in person; Britannica notes its reputation for having the best cavalry in Europe. Sinor judges an accurate estimate of the Mongol army impossible, and no army sizes are used here.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: The right wing campaigned in Poland and on 9 April 1241 destroyed the army of Henry II, duke of Silesia, at Liegnitz (Legnica). Sinor names the Carpathian passes used, among them Borgo, Oituz, the Olt defile and Verecke; Batu chose to enter Hungary from the north, through the “Russian gate”. Britannica has the main force destroy the Hungarian defences in the Carpathians and sweep across Hungary to the Sajó, where Béla encamped on the opposite bank.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: Britannica places the attack on 10 April. Batu and his brother Shiban attacked frontally across the river while Subutai rode north to find a ford. They made little headway until catapult-fired projectiles drove the Hungarians back; once across, they turned the Hungarian position and drew up in single file. Subutai's troops then appeared behind the Hungarians, who charged out to regain their camp. Subutai bombarded the camp and sent in his heavy cavalry, and a column fleeing toward Pest was pursued and shot down by mounted archers. Sinor dates the decisive action to 11 April and describes it as a night attack by Batu's forces on the Hungarian camp. Pow and Laszlovszky note that several sources agree that some of the heaviest fighting took place as the Mongols struggled to force the bridge over the Sajó, and that the Mongols sought to conceal their crossing in order to encircle the camp before dawn.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: In Britannica's account the Mongol plan divided the attack: a frontal crossing to hold the Hungarians in place and a flank crossing to strike them from behind. Two unrelated thirteenth-century sources, Thomas of Split and the Persian historian Juvayni, describe Batu climbing a hill before the battle: for Thomas to view the Hungarian camp, for Juvayni to pray, after Shiban's reconnaissance had reported the Hungarian army much larger than his own. Béla's choices before the battle shaped his position: he had admitted the Cumans, whom he lost just as the Mongols arrived, and he relied on help from Frederick of Austria that never came.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: Two moments decided the battle in Britannica's account: the use of projectiles to force the river crossing, and the arrival of Subutai's force behind the Hungarian camp, which turned a defence of the river line into an attempt to break out. The pursuit toward Pest then turned defeat into the destruction of the army.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The Hungarian army was destroyed, with heavy losses among the nobility; Sinor notes that some call it a massacre rather than a battle. Béla escaped with great difficulty. Britannica's battle article says he took refuge in Croatia and its biography of him says Dalmatia; Sinor has him find shelter on an island facing Trogir. The Mongols burned Pest and massacred its inhabitants.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: For about a year, Britannica's biography of Béla says, the kingdom of Hungary did not exist; Hungarians still use the word tatárjárás, Tatar invasion, for total calamity. Mongol detachments pursued Béla into Dalmatia and Croatia, in raids that Sinor finds hampered by poor pasture, and the withdrawal from Hungary was complete by May 1242. Béla rebuilt his kingdom, including a network of fortifications, fought to recover the western lands Frederick of Austria had seized, and turned back a second Mongol invasion in 1261.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Widely separated forces can act as one plan when their timing is coordinated: the Polish thrust and the invasion of Hungary struck within days of each other. A river line protects a camp only while every crossing is watched. A defender's internal divisions, here between the kingdom and the Cumans it had sheltered, can open before the enemy arrives.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The sources disagree on the date (10 April in Britannica, 11 April in Sinor) and on the form of the attack: Britannica describes a frontal crossing with “catapult-fired explosives” and a flank attack, Sinor a night attack on the camp; the weapons Britannica names are not described in the other sources read. The main debate concerns the withdrawal of 1242. Britannica's battle article attributes it to the death of the Great Khan Ögedei and the need to choose a successor, and its biography of Béla to dynastic troubles. Sinor, noting that Ögedei died on 11 December 1241, calls this explanation, which goes back to Carpini, a mistake and argues that the withdrawal was caused by logistical imperatives, above all the limited pasture of the Hungarian plain for the Mongols' horses. Hungarian research has turned to the ground itself: Pow and Laszlovszky combine the chronicles of Thomas of Split and Master Roger with Asian sources, which they judge more reliable for the Mongol side, and with battlefield archaeology, and offer a reconstruction they themselves call hypothetical, in which Batu may have watched the Hungarian camp from a burial mound some distance from the bridge and prayed on the hills near Szerencs. Figures for both armies vary widely and are not used.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Denis Sinor's article, published in the Journal of Asian History and reproduced by De Re Militari, gives the Mongol command structure, the chronology of the western campaign and the argument about pasture and withdrawal. Charles Phillips's Britannica article gives the most detailed tactical narrative but does not cite its sources. Britannica's biography of Béla IV covers the aftermath in Hungary. Stephen Pow and József Laszlovszky's article in the Hungarian Historical Review, part of a Hungarian research project on the battle, brings together the European and Asian sources and recent archaeological work on the battlefield. The contemporary chronicles themselves were not read for this study.

perspectives.objective: Defeat the Hungarian army and open the Hungarian plain to the Mongol forces.
perspectives.known: The Hungarian army lay encamped across the Sajó; Britannica credits him with planning the three-pronged invasion and its supporting campaign in Poland.

perspectives.name: Béla IV
perspectives.objective: Defend the kingdom of Hungary against the Mongol invasion.
perspectives.known: Kiev had fallen in December 1240, and Mongol forces had broken through the Carpathian defences and crossed the plain.
perspectives.uncertainty: The loyalty of the Cumans he had admitted, which became a matter of mob suspicion, and whether Frederick of Austria's promised help would come.
perspectives.constraints: The loss of the Cumans after Koten's murder, and help from Austria that never arrived.
perspectives.forces: The Hungarian royal army, renowned for its cavalry, with the nobility of the kingdom.
perspectives.terrain: A camp on the bank of the Sajó, facing the Mongols across the river.
perspectives.logistics: The sources read do not describe his supply, so it is not reconstructed here.
perspectives.decision: He encamped facing the Mongols across the Sajó; when they appeared behind his camp, his army tried to break out, and he fled.
perspectives.outcome: His army was destroyed; he escaped to the Adriatic coast, returned after the Mongol withdrawal and rebuilt the kingdom.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: Toyotomi Hideyoshi, who had reunited Japan by 1591, ordered an invasion of Ming China through Korea in 1592. Busan, Korea's most important port, fell on 24 May 1592, and the invasion began from there. The Encyclopedia of Korean Culture describes the Japanese plan as a combined advance by land and sea.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Most of the Korean military was unprepared, but Yi Sun-sin, appointed commander of the Left Jeolla naval forces in 1591, had trained his men, stocked equipment and supplies and developed the turtle ship (kŏbuksŏn). Japanese fleets moving along the south coast were defeated at Okpo, Dangpo, Danghangpo and Yulpo. In response Wakisaka Yasuharu, an able naval commander, reinforced his fleet with picked troops and moved against Geoje, with Kuki Yoshitaka following with a second squadron.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: The Japanese aimed to push their fleets along the south coast in support of the advance by land; the encyclopedia presents Wakisaka's sortie as an answer to the earlier defeats. Yi aimed to find and destroy the main Japanese fleet. Britannica judges that the effect of his victories was to cut the Japanese in Korea off from supplies and reinforcements.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The Japanese fleet lay in Gyeonnaeryang, a strait off Geoje Island. Yi judged it too narrow and too full of reefs for his panokseon warships to move freely, and chose instead the open water off Hansan Island.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Yi Sun-sin, commander of the Left Jeolla fleet, sailed with Yi Eok-gi, commander of the Right Jeolla fleet, and joined Won Gyun, commander of the Right Gyeongsang fleet, to form a combined fleet of the three provinces. Its main warships were panokseon, which fought with cannon such as the Ji- and Hyeon-ja chongtong; Britannica describes Yi's armoured turtle ships, with cannon at bow, stern and sides. Wakisaka Yasuharu commanded the Japanese fleet at Gyeonnaeryang.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: On the 5th day of the 7th lunar month Yi Sun-sin and Yi Eok-gi assembled the Jeolla fleets off Yeosu for joint training. They sailed the next day and joined Won Gyun's ships at Noryang. On the evening of the 7th, off Dangpo, a herdboy, Kim Cheon-son, told them that a Japanese fleet was anchored in Gyeonnaeryang, and on the 8th, off Hansan Island, they confirmed it.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: Five or six panokseon attacked the Japanese fleet and, when it counter-attacked, fell back toward Hansan Island, drawing it out of the strait. The encyclopedia describes the Japanese as coming on in high spirits, as if to avenge their earlier defeats. In the open water Yi had the whole fleet form the crane-wing formation (hagikjin) and attack, firing cannon as they closed. Most of the Japanese ships were burned or captured, and survivors abandoned their ships and fled ashore. The Japanese compilation Seikan iryaku, quoting the Korean minister Ryu Seong-ryong's Jingbirok, describes the same feigned withdrawal, the Korean ships turning together at a drumbeat once the Japanese were clear of the narrows, turtle ships firing on every side, and the tall turreted Japanese flagships broken by cannon; Wakisaka barely escaped to Gimhae. The next day the combined fleet won again at Angolpo; the Seikan iryaku has Kuki's and Katō's squadron attacked by a large Korean fleet and fighting from morning to evening.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Yi's first decision was not to fight in Gyeonnaeryang, where the strait limited his ships, but to lure the enemy into open water with a small decoy force. His second was to turn the whole fleet into the crane-wing formation once the Japanese had followed, and to close with cannon fire.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The battle was decided when the Japanese fleet followed the decoy out of the strait: in the open water the Joseon fleet could deploy in formation and use its guns, which the narrow, reef-filled strait would not have allowed.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The battle was a major Joseon victory. Most of the Japanese fleet was burned or captured, and some of its men escaped ashore. The Joseon fleet suffered casualties but lost no ships. For Hansan and Angolpo Yi Sun-sin was promoted to the senior second rank, and Yi Eok-gi and Won Gyun were also promoted.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The encyclopedia counts Hansan, with the defence of Jinju in 1592 and the victory at Haengju in 1593, among the three great victories of the Imjin War. By destroying most of the main Japanese fleet it frustrated the combined land and sea plan, lifted the morale of Korean forces beaten on land and secured Joseon control of the waters along the south coast, a threat to the Japanese already ashore. Britannica concludes that Yi's victories off the southern coast cut the Japanese in Korea off from supplies and reinforcements and kept them from pressing their initial advantage. In 1593 Yi was given command of the entire Korean fleet.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Choosing where to fight can matter more than numbers: Yi declined battle in waters that suited the enemy and created one in waters that suited his ships. Preparation before the war, in training, supplies and ships, made that choice possible.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The encyclopedia's narrative rests on Korean records, among them the Annals of King Seonjo and Yi Sun-sin's collected works and reports, with a 1924 Japanese General Staff history among its references. The Japanese side is read here in Kawaguchi Chōju's Seikan iryaku, a nineteenth-century Japanese history of the invasions written in Classical Chinese, which calls the Japanese “our troops” and draws both on Japanese family records and on Ryu's Jingbirok. From the Japanese records it adds that Wakisaka, angered by the defeat, attacked Yi again and took his ships, a claim it takes from Wakisaka's epitaph and a genealogy and which the Korean sources read here do not mention; it also has some Korean ships at the next day's fighting clad in iron that Japanese shot could not harm. The date is given in the lunar calendar of the Korean sources; it is not the same day in the Western calendar, and no source read gives the converted date. Hulbert's comparison with Salamis, quoted in the encyclopedia, and his view that the battle sealed the fate of Hideyoshi's invasion are retrospective judgements. Britannica writes that the turtle ship is thought to have been the first ironclad. The encyclopedia's account of Hansan names the panokseon and does not mention turtle ships, but Ryu's account, as the Seikan iryaku quotes it, places them in this battle.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Jo Seong-do's entry in the Encyclopedia of Korean Culture, published by the Academy of Korean Studies, gives the day-by-day narrative from Korean records. Britannica's biography of Yi Sun-shin gives his preparations and the strategic effect of his victories, and Stephen Turnbull's Britannica article on the siege of Busanjin gives the opening of the invasion. Kawaguchi Chōju's Seikan iryaku, in Classical Chinese on Wikisource, gives the Japanese account, combining Japanese family records with the Korean Jingbirok.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: In 1575, during Japan's Age of Warring States, Takeda Katsuyori besieged Nagashino castle in Mikawa, held for Tokugawa Ieyasu. The small garrison held out, Kobayashi writes, for nearly twenty days. Two years earlier the Takeda had soundly defeated the Tokugawa at Mikatagahara.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Oda Nobunaga, Ieyasu's ally, marched to relieve the castle. The Takeda-side chronicles say he came only reluctantly: twice he refused Ieyasu's appeals, and moved only when Ieyasu's third envoy, Oguri Dairoku, warned that Ieyasu would otherwise make peace with Katsuyori and join him against Nobunaga's province of Owari. Kobayashi notes that Nobunaga controlled Sakai, a centre of the matchlock trade. Citing the historian Hirayama Yū, he adds that Sakai, a hub of foreign trade, gave Nobunaga ready access to the lead and saltpetre needed for shot and powder, which the inland Takeda of Kai lacked, and that Nobunaga may have imposed an economic blockade.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Katsuyori sought to take Nagashino from the Tokugawa. Nobunaga aimed to relieve it and to defeat the army that had beaten the Tokugawa two years before, on ground he had prepared; Kobayashi describes the Takeda as drawn out to Shitaragahara to meet him.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The allies took position at Shitaragahara, which Kobayashi describes as a long north–south hollow. The Aichi Prefecture account places the stockade along the foot of the escarpment of a middle river terrace of the Toyokawa, where it meets the alluvial flat of the Rengo stream; a reconstruction stands on the original line. The Takeda deployed on an older, higher terrace across the stream. It was the rainy season, and the Takeda had to descend the escarpment and cross the muddy flat under fire from the stockade. Britannica places the palisade between the forested edge of the hills and the river.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Takeda Katsuyori led the Takeda army, whose commanders included senior retainers from Takeda Shingen's time such as Yamagata Masakage, whose unit wore red armour, and Baba Nobuharu. Oda Nobunaga and Tokugawa Ieyasu commanded the allied army, which included a large body of matchlock musketeers; Britannica describes it as vastly outnumbering the Takeda. Hirayama, as Kobayashi reports, finds that the Takeda also had many guns but lacked shot and powder. Army sizes and the number of guns are disputed and are not used here.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Nobunaga had a palisade built to protect his musketeers: Britannica describes a loose fence of stakes in three staggered layers, with gaps for counter-attacks, along a front of about two kilometres. Kobayashi notes that the Naruse version of the Nagashino battle screen shows the fence as hastily built and flimsy, with many soldiers outside it. The Tokugawa held the right, northern wing, facing the main Takeda force; Kobayashi suggests the Takeda aimed first to break the Tokugawa.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: During the siege the besiegers tried attacks by river, mining and assault. Britannica tells how Torii Suneemon, a junior samurai, slipped out to reach Ieyasu's army at Okazaki; captured on his way back, he shouted to the garrison that help was coming before he was killed. The allied army took position at Shitaragahara, and the Takeda moved out to face it. In the battle Nobunaga's musketeers fired volleys as the Takeda approached and broke the charge, but the Takeda fought on until mid-afternoon, when they began to retreat and were pursued. The Kōyō gunkan describes each Takeda corps driving its opponents back behind the stockade, Yamagata Masakage trying to work round the Tokugawa flank before he was shot, and the Sanada brothers killed trying to break through one line of the fence. Kobayashi names senior Takeda commanders killed while covering Katsuyori's retreat: Yamagata Masakage, Hara Masatane, Tsuchiya Masatsugu and Baba Nobuharu, who commanded the rearguard.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Nobunaga chose to meet the Takeda from a fortified line, with a palisade and massed matchlocks; Obata's memorandum credits the idea of ditches, a stockade and massed guns to a retainer named Saitō, and says the triple stockade was put up overnight. It also has Sakai Tadatsugu propose a night attack on the Takeda fort at Tobinosu; Nobunaga rebuked him in council, then privately sent him to carry it out. On the Takeda side, both chronicles say the senior retainers, Baba, Naitō and Yamagata among them, urged Katsuyori not to fight, proposing a withdrawal to fight on home ground or a quick storm of the castle instead. Katsuyori, backed by Nagasaka Chōkan and Atobe Katsusuke, decided to attack and swore on the house's sacred banner and armour, after which no one could object. He later withdrew when his army was overwhelmed. Kobayashi reports a theory that the flimsy fence was a deliberate trap, made to look weak to invite a Takeda charge; it remains a theory.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The Takeda attacks broke down at the fence line, where the muddy flat of the stream slowed them under fire. The deaths of senior commanders while covering the retreat turned a repulse into a disaster for the Takeda house.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The battle ended, in Kobayashi's words, in the destruction of the Takeda army. Katsuyori withdrew. Britannica records very heavy Takeda losses, including many senior leaders, and comparatively few on the allied side.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Katsuyori survived, but seven years later, cornered by Nobunaga, he killed himself and the Takeda house was destroyed. Britannica calls Nagashino the first modern Japanese battle because of Nobunaga's use of firearms and says it revolutionised Japanese warfare. Its further claim, that the battle signalled the last days of the Ashikaga shogunate, is a long-range judgement.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Firepower depends on supply: Nobunaga's hold on the trade in guns, lead and saltpetre mattered as much as the guns on the field. Simple field fortifications, sited where the ground slowed the attacker, multiplied the effect of fire.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The traditional picture of massed musketeers firing in three alternating ranks against a Takeda cavalry charge is contested. Kobayashi notes that the number of guns differs between manuscripts of the Shinchō kōki, the primary-source chronicle of Nobunaga's life, and that a later account, the Tōdaiki, has mercenaries from Negoro and Saiga bring guns of their own, so the real number is unclear. The Naruse screen shows no three-rank formation, and the ground is said not to allow one; a newer view holds that gunners worked in groups of three so that one was always ready to fire. Britannica, written by Stephen Turnbull, keeps the volley account. Hirayama's argument that the Takeda lacked shot and powder rather than guns moves the explanation from tactics to supply. The battle screens were made decades later and are depictions, not eyewitness evidence. The two Takeda-side texts read here are house tradition: the Kōyō gunkan claims that the Takeda won every individual clash at the fence and lays the decision to fight on Katsuyori's favourites Nagasaka and Atobe, and both give figures that are not used. Their triple stockade matches Britannica's three layers. The Western date, 28 June, is Britannica's; Kobayashi and the Kōyō gunkan give the 21st day of the 5th month in the Japanese calendar.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Stephen Turnbull's Britannica article gives the siege and the standard account of the battle. Kobayashi Akira's article for nippon.com, built around the Naruse battle screen and Hirayama Yū's work, gives the Japanese debate on the guns, the fence and supply. The Aichi Prefecture page on the battlefield describes the terrain and the rebuilt stockade. The Takeda side is read in chapter 52 of the Kōyō gunkan and in Obata Kagenori's memorandum on the battle, both in Japanese on Wikisource. The Shinchō kōki itself was not read.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: Nader's victory at Damghan in 1729 consolidated his control of Iran, and he became shah in 1736. In 1738 he destroyed Qandahar, the last stronghold of the Ghilzai Afghans who had ended Safavid rule, completing the recovery of lost territory. Tucker writes that his pursuit of Afghans who had fled across the Mughal frontier grew into an invasion of India when he accused the Mughals of sheltering and aiding them.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: The Mughal Empire had been weakened by wars and internal strife since Aurangzeb's death in 1707. Under Muhammad Shah, emperor from 1719, the provinces slipped out of imperial control: Sa'adat Khan made himself practically independent in Oudh, Bengal paid only an annual tribute, and the Marathas raided Delhi in 1737. Britannica's biography of the emperor says Nader took advantage of Mughal neglect of the North-West Frontier.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Tucker presents the invasion as the start of a new phase in Nader's career, the pursuit of a world empire on the model of Chinggis Khan and Timur, as well as a punitive pursuit. The Mughal aim was to stop the invader north of Delhi, where the army lay encamped near Karnal.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Karnal lies in northern India, north of Delhi, on the old highway from the Punjab. Jadunath Sarkar, drawing on the Mughal and Persian chronicles, explains why the Mughal army stopped there: Ali Mardan's canal gave abundant water and the plain around offered room for large bodies of cavalry. The Jamuna ran a few miles to the east. Britannica describes a Mughal front more than 3 km long and as deep.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Nader led a disciplined army that, Tucker notes, included many Afghans who had joined him after Qandahar. Muhammad Shah's army included war elephants; its chief commanders included Khan Dauran and Sa'adat Khan. Britannica describes the Mughal army as the larger; army sizes vary between accounts and are not used here.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Sarkar writes that the emperor's advisers, above all the Nizam, decided to entrench at Karnal rather than risk a battle, enclosing the camp with a mud wall many miles round and lining it with guns, while they waited for Saadat Khan's contingent from Oudh. Nader avoided a frontal attack: he marched round to the east, keeping to the Jamuna's water and threatening Panipat in the Mughal rear, so as to force the emperor out of his lines or march on Delhi past him. On 24 February, in Britannica's dating, the Persians advanced toward Karnal, and the Mughals sent a huge force, including war elephants, to meet them.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: In Sarkar's account Saadat Khan reached the camp at midnight, and the next morning, while a council of war sat with the emperor, news came that Persian skirmishers had fallen on his baggage. Against the advice of the Nizam and Khan Dauran, who urged waiting a day, he rode out with only part of his men; Khan Dauran followed to support him, and the emperor drew up beside the canal more as a spectator than a combatant, so that the three Mughal divisions stood more than a mile apart. The Persians waited until the Mughal force came within close range and then fired devastating volleys, the elephants making especially easy targets: Persian skirmishers feigned flight and drew Saadat Khan onto massed swivel-guns. Khan Dauran was seriously wounded and forced to retire, dying the next day, and Sa'adat Khan was pulled from his elephant and captured. After two hours the Mughal lines began to fall apart and the soldiers fled back to their camp. The battle swiftly became a rout; Nader did not assault the fortified camp itself.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Britannica describes Nader's troops as holding their fire until the Mughal force was at close range. Sarkar adds the manoeuvre that made the battle possible, Nader's march round the camp, and the Mughal decisions that lost it: Saadat Khan's rush to save his baggage, the piecemeal commitment of Khan Dauran's division, and the inaction of the Nizam, the ablest Mughal general, who gave no help, perhaps, as one chronicler suggested, hoping to take his rivals' places at court. After the battle Nader chose to keep Muhammad Shah on the throne as his vassal rather than depose him.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The loss of two chief commanders early in the fighting, one wounded and one captured, weakened the Mughal army just as its lines came under fire, and the break after two hours became a rout.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The Mughal army was routed. Britannica says the Persians captured Muhammad Shah; Tucker writes that Nader made him his vassal. Persian troops occupied Delhi. When a rumour spread that Nader had been assassinated, inhabitants attacked and killed his soldiers, and in retaliation he gave his army permission to plunder the city and massacre its people.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Nader took much of the Mughal treasury, including the Peacock Throne and the Koh-i-Noor diamond, with horses, elephants and skilled artisans. The peace treaty restored Muhammad Shah under Nader's distant suzerainty; Nader placed the crown back on his head and took the title shahanshah. The wealth let Nader cancel all taxes in Iran for three years, though he later had to reinstate them, and the heavy levies sparked rebellions. Britannica judges that Karnal marked the effective end of the Mughal Empire, whose decline became terminal; Muhammad Shah reigned until 1748 and that year defeated Ahmad Shah Durrani at Sirhind.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Fire discipline can outweigh numbers: an army that held its fire until the enemy was close broke a larger one. A state whose provinces have slipped from its control may still field a large army, but a single defeat can expose how little lies behind it.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Britannica says the Persians captured Muhammad Shah; Tucker writes only that Nader made him his vassal, and the sources read do not describe how the emperor came to submit. Britannica's statement that Karnal marked the effective end of the Mughal Empire is a strong retrospective judgement: in its own account the emperor kept his throne, and its biography of him records a victory at Sirhind in 1748. Tucker notes that Nader's chroniclers presented the victory as another sign of his likeness to Timur, which is the court's view of it. Tucker gives both the pursuit of Afghan fugitives and wider imperial ambition as motives for the invasion. Sarkar dates the battle to 13 February 1739 and Britannica to 24 February, eleven days apart, which matches the difference between the Old Style and New Style calendars. Britannica has the Mughals send a huge force out to meet the Persians; Sarkar describes a battle the Mughal commanders did not plan, brought on by Saadat Khan's sortie, and notes that his own sources disagree on whether the emperor ordered it. Sarkar, writing in the 1920s, explains the defeat by weapons and tactics, Persian firearms and mobility against Indian swordsmen and elephants, as well as by generalship; his sweeping generalisations about peoples are of his time and are not adopted here. Army sizes and losses vary between accounts and are not used.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Jacob F. Field's Britannica article gives the narrative of the battle. Ernest Tucker's Encyclopaedia Iranica article on Nader Shah gives the Iranian side: the road to the invasion, the settlement with Muhammad Shah and its effects in Iran. Britannica's biography of Muhammad Shah gives the state of the Mughal Empire. Jadunath Sarkar's Nadir Shah in India, based on the Persian and Mughal chronicles, which he cites, gives the Mughal side of the campaign and the battle. The chronicles themselves were not read for this study.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: Rome and Sasanian Iran had contested the Middle East for centuries. Procopius describes renewed fighting in the 520s: Roman raids into Persarmenia under Sittas and Belisarius, then young bodyguards of Justinian, and a failed advance near Nisibis, after which Belisarius was given command of the troops at Dara. When Belisarius began a fort at Mindouos on the frontier, the Persians forbade the work, defeated the Romans sent to protect it and razed what had been built. The Syriac chronicle attributed to Zachariah of Mitylene gives a local version of that defeat: in the desert of Thannuris the Persians dug concealed pits around their entrenchment, Roman generals rode into them and were captured, and Belisarius fled to Dara with the cavalry while the infantry was killed or taken.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Justinian, sole emperor from 527, made Belisarius General of the East. Hermogenes, holding the office of magister, came to help him set the army in order, and the envoy Rufinus waited at Hierapolis on the Euphrates, for, Procopius writes, there was already much talk of peace on both sides. Iranica places the battle within an indecisive war fought in Lazica, Armenia, northern Mesopotamia and Syria.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Warned that the Persians meant to take Dara, Belisarius and Hermogenes chose to fight before the city rather than wait behind its walls. The Persian commander, whose title Procopius gives as mirranes and whose name as Perozes, aimed to take the city; Procopius has him send word that Belisarius should prepare a bath for him in it.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: About a stone's throw from the gate facing Nisibis, the Romans dug a deep trench with many crossings: a short straight centre section, cross trenches at right angles from each end, and from those two long straight trenches continuing in the original direction. A hill rose at the left end of the line. The Persians camped at Ammodios, twenty stades from Dara.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Belisarius and Hermogenes stood behind the centre of the trench. On the left Bouzes held the end of the trench with cavalry, together with Pharas and his Heruli, and at the left angle stood the Massagetae horsemen of Sunicas and Aigan. On the right were John son of Nicetas with Cyril, Marcellus, Germanus and Dorotheus, and at the right angle the horsemen of Simmas and Ascan. The mirranes commanded the Persians, with Pityaxes and Baresmanas leading the wings and the so-called Immortals in reserve. Britannica notes that Belisarius had been given a command at about the age of 25. Procopius gives figures for both armies, with the Persians the larger; they are not used here.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: On the first day the armies faced each other until late afternoon, when a Persian detachment attacked Bouzes and Pharas, who fell back and then drove it off. Andreas, a wrestling trainer attending Bouzes, killed two Persian champions in single combat, the second against Hermogenes' orders, and the Persians withdrew to Ammodios. The next day Persian reinforcements arrived from Nisibis, and the commanders exchanged letters, the Romans urging withdrawal and peace and the mirranes refusing.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: On the day of battle the mirranes put only half his army in line, so that the rest could relieve the fighters in turn, and held the Immortals back; he stood in the centre, with Pityaxes on the right and Baresmanas on the left. Pharas proposed hiding the Heruli behind the hill to fall on the Persian rear, and Belisarius agreed. The Persians attacked after midday. Arrows flew thickly, a steady wind blunting the Persian volleys, until the armies closed with spears. On the Roman left the Cadiseni under Pityaxes broke through, but the Heruli struck them from the hill behind and Sunicas and Aigan charged their flank, and the Persian right fled. The mirranes then sent many men and the Immortals to his left. Belisarius and Hermogenes moved Sunicas and Aigan to the right angle with many of Belisarius's own men behind them, and when Baresmanas and the Immortals drove back the Roman right, the men at the angle charged into their flank and cut them in two. Sunicas killed Baresmanas, the Persian left broke, and the Persian infantry threw down their shields and were cut down. Zachariah's chronicle tells the battle more briefly: the Persians came up on the south side of the city to blockade it, and Sunicas, a baptized Hun, and a tribune it names Simuth, probably Procopius's Simmas as the translators suggest, each with a few followers, drove them from the walls several times, while the Heruli under Bouzes threw back the Persian infantry east of the city.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: The trench, shaped so that the wings could give ground while the angles struck from the side, was prepared before the Persians arrived. During the battle Belisarius and Hermogenes accepted Pharas's plan for an ambush from the hill and moved their reserve from the left angle to the right when they saw the Persians shifting troops. They then stopped the pursuit after a short distance, fearing that the Persians might turn on men pursuing recklessly and judging it enough to keep the victory intact.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The two flank counter-attacks decided the battle: the Heruli and Sunicas's horsemen broke the Persian right, and the reserve moved to the right angle cut through the attack of the Immortals. The death of Baresmanas and the fall of his standard broke the Persian left.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The Persian army was routed with heavy losses. Procopius writes that the Persians had been defeated in battle by the Romans, a thing which had not happened for a long time, and that afterwards they were no longer willing to fight a pitched battle there, though sudden attacks continued on both sides. Zachariah adds that the Persians sent to Nisibis for pack animals to carry away their dead, and that the rest of their army went on to burn Roman territory in Arabia. Britannica calls it a brilliant victory, Belisarius's first as a commander.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Belisarius was defeated the following year at Sura (Callinicum) but, Britannica writes, emerged as the hero of the war by the time Justinian negotiated its end. In 532 Khosrow I and Justinian agreed an unlimited peace: Dara stayed Roman, though no longer as the military headquarters for Mesopotamia, and Byzantium agreed to pay toward the Persian defence of the Caucasus. Belisarius was sent against the Vandals in 533. When war resumed in 540, Khosrow extorted ransom from Dara among other towns.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: A prepared position can shape an enemy's attack: the trench fixed where the Persians could press, and its angles let reserves strike from the side. Reserves are most useful when they can be moved to where the enemy commits his own.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Procopius was chosen as Belisarius's adviser at Dara, and Britannica notes that he served on the general's staff for the first fifteen years of his campaigns and observed them himself; that gives his account authority but also a reason to favour his general. The speeches and letters he gives the commanders are his compositions, and his explanation of the Persians' timing, attacking after noon because the Romans ate earlier, is his own. Zachariah's Syriac chronicle, an independent account, gives the credit to Sunicas and Simuth rather than to the general's plan and does not mention the trench, the ambush from the hill or the reserve moved between the angles; it ascribes the deliverance to God and calls the Persians boastful. Procopius's numbers for both armies and for the Persian dead are not used. Britannica calls Dara a brilliant victory, while Iranica treats the whole war as indecisive, since the peace of 532 left the frontier much as it had been. The month is given in the margin of Dewing's translation, not in Procopius's text.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Procopius's History of the Wars, in H. B. Dewing's Loeb translation on Project Gutenberg, gives the narrative this study follows. The Syriac chronicle attributed to Zachariah of Mitylene, in Hamilton and Brooks's translation of 1899 on the Internet Archive, gives a briefer, independent account. John Walton Barker's Britannica biography gives Belisarius's career, and A. Shapur Shahbazi's article on Byzantine–Iranian relations in Encyclopaedia Iranica places the war in the long rivalry of the two empires. No Persian account was read.
