perspectives.name: Belisarius
perspectives.objective: Defend Dara against the Persian army that had come to take it.
perspectives.known: The Persians were camped at Ammodios, twenty stades away, and their commander had announced that he would bathe in the city.
perspectives.uncertainty: Whether his men would keep their order at close quarters; the speech Procopius gives the Roman generals blames an earlier defeat on soldiers heedless of their officers.
perspectives.constraints: Command shared with Hermogenes, sent by the emperor, while peace talks were under way and an envoy waited at Hierapolis.
perspectives.forces: Cavalry and infantry along the trench, Massagetae and Herul horsemen on the flanks, and his own men in reserve.
perspectives.terrain: A shaped trench before the city gate, with crossings, angles for flank attacks and a hill at the left end.
perspectives.logistics: Fighting before the walls of Dara, his men could withdraw inside the fortifications at night, as they did after the first day.
perspectives.decision: He fought from the trench, accepted Pharas's plan for an ambush from the hill, moved his reserve to the right angle and halted the pursuit.
perspectives.outcome: A victory that, Procopius writes, the Romans had not won over the Persians for a long time.

perspectives.name: Perozes, the mirranes
perspectives.objective: Take Dara; Zachariah says the Persians came up to the south side of the city meaning to blockade it.
perspectives.known: The Romans had dug in before the city and on the first day had kept their order.
perspectives.uncertainty: Whether the Roman order would hold at close quarters; in the speech Procopius gives him he argued that it would not.
perspectives.constraints: An attack against a prepared line in front of a strong city.
perspectives.forces: A larger army of horse and foot, with the Immortals in reserve and reinforcements from Nisibis.
perspectives.terrain: A trench with crossings and flanking angles, and a hill at the Roman left that hid the Heruli.
perspectives.logistics: His army came from Nisibis and camped at Ammodios; the sources read do not describe its supply.
perspectives.decision: He fought in relays with half his army, attacked after midday and moved the Immortals to his left for a second blow.
perspectives.outcome: Both his wings were broken and his infantry cut down; Procopius writes that the Persians would no longer meet the Romans in pitched battle there, and Zachariah that they carried their dead back to Nisibis.

sources.title: Battle of Arsūf
Battle of Arsuf
Behâ ed-Dîn, The Life of Saladin
Itinerary of Richard I, attributed to Geoffrey de Vinsauf, in Chronicles of the Crusades (London: Bohn, 1848)

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: Richard I took Acre in July 1191 and marched south along the coast toward Jaffa. Baha al-Din, who was with Saladin, writes that the sultan was enraged by the massacre of the Muslim prisoners at Acre, which a captured knight blamed on the king alone; during the march Saladin had Frankish prisoners put to death.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Saladin's army shadowed the crusaders and slowed them with attacks on their flanks. Baha al-Din records that the Franks made short marches because the infantry not fighting carried the baggage and tents, that their ships followed along the coast, and that they halted to await the fleet with men and supplies. Before the battle Richard met Saladin's brother al-Adil and demanded the return of all the territory; al-Adil refused, and Saladin told his brother to draw out the talks until Turkoman reinforcements arrived.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Richard aimed to reach Jaffa as a base for an advance on Jerusalem. Saladin aimed to wear the army down on the march and, as Baha al-Din writes, to provoke its knights into charging so that his men could attack them.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The road ran south along the coast between the sea and wooded country. Baha al-Din names the river camps of the march and the wood of Arsuf, where Saladin's troops once lost their way at night; the battle came as the crusaders approached the thickets and gardens of Arsuf. Britannica describes the attacks growing heavier after the crusaders left the forest of Arsuf.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Baha al-Din, who watched the march, describes the crusader infantry drawn up in front of the cavalry, “firm as a wall”, in thick felt and mail that arrows could not pierce, with crossbows that wounded Muslim horses and riders. One division of infantry fought while the other rested along the shore, and the cavalry, in three divisions, kept to the centre and left it only to charge. Libertini likewise describes the cavalry kept between columns of infantry to shield the horses. The crusader Itinerary gives the order of march on the day: Templars in front, then the Bretons and Angevins, King Guy with the Poitevins, the Normans and English guarding the royal standard, and the Hospitallers in the rear, with bowmen and crossbowmen on the outside and the baggage between the army and the sea. Saladin's army relied on mounted archers and attacks from every side, with the sultan riding among his squadrons. Figures for the two armies, modern and medieval, vary and are not used.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: On 7 September the crusaders marched toward Arsuf. Saladin drew up his army for battle, resolved, Baha al-Din writes, to come to close quarters that day; his archers advanced and attacked the column on every side, some divisions led by the sultan while others stood in reserve. Britannica says the attacks were concentrated against the Hospitallers in the rear guard.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: Under the arrows the crusaders hurried on toward their halting place, and the Muslims began to think the victory would be easy. The Itinerary describes the crossbowmen giving way under the pressure, knights who had lost their horses fighting on foot, and the Hospitallers in the rear so hard pressed that their master twice asked Richard for leave to charge; Richard told him to hold. When the crusader infantry reached the gardens of Arsuf, the knights gathered within the infantry, which opened to let them through, and charged; Baha al-Din saw the charge strike the Muslim right, left and centre, which all fled. Britannica has the Hospitallers, who had lost many horses, break ranks and counter-attack, and Richard reinforce them with a general charge. Saladin rallied his men around his own squadron and drums; the crusaders charged three times, halted on the high ground and fell back toward their camp, fearing an ambush in the woods.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Richard held his cavalry back under prolonged attack, Britannica says in the hope of drawing out the main Muslim army; the Itinerary says a charge had been agreed for a signal of six trumpets in the van, centre and rear. When the Hospitallers broke ranks, he committed the whole army behind them, and he did not pursue far for fear of ambush. Saladin chose to attack the column as it neared Arsuf and, when his army broke, stood with his own squadron and kept the drums beating to rally the fugitives.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The charge, once launched, broke all three parts of Saladin's army at once. The sultan's stand with his squadron and the crusaders' halt for fear of ambush kept the defeat from becoming the destruction of his army.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The crusaders held the field and went on to Jaffa. Baha al-Din calls the battle a blow to all Muslim hearts and describes Saladin overwhelmed by the day; both sides had many killed and wounded, several of Saladin's emirs were among the dead, and Arabs who went over the field counted more than a hundred dead crusader horses. The Itinerary mourns the death of James d'Avesnes, killed when his companions failed to support him, and says the Turks' line of flight could be traced by abandoned baggage and dead horses and camels. Casualty figures in the modern and medieval accounts are not used.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Saladin regrouped and in the next days offered battle again near Arsuf and harassed the march, but the crusaders would not charge and continued to the river 'Auja and to Jaffa, which, prisoners told Saladin, they meant to fortify. Britannica judges the victory no crushing blow: from 9 September the harassment resumed and Richard did not dare push on to Jerusalem. Libertini links the battle to Saladin's later acceptance of a truce that secured crusader control of the coast.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Discipline on the march can defeat an army built to break it: the crusader column absorbed days of archery because its infantry shielded the horses. A counter-stroke works best when the enemy has committed to close action, and at Arsuf the charge, planned or not, came at that moment.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The sources disagree on how the charge began. Britannica has the Hospitallers break ranks and Richard follow with a general charge, Libertini presents a charge that Richard held back until conditions favoured it, and Baha al-Din, who saw it from the Muslim centre, describes the knights forming within the infantry and charging together; his 1897 editor notes that the charge began with the Hospitallers in the rear. The crusader Itinerary settles part of the question from the other side: it says the leaders had agreed on a charge at a trumpet signal, but that two knights, the marshal of the Hospitallers and Baldwin de Carreo, rode out before it, so that the charge came early and in disorder; it judges that the Turks would otherwise have been utterly defeated. It also gives Saladin a speech reproaching his emirs, which the chronicler cannot have heard. Baha al-Din writes that the knights resolved to charge knowing that only a supreme effort could save them, which is his reading of their situation, and his editor notes that he minimises Muslim losses; the Itinerary, for its part, magnifies the enemy and the Christian heroism. Britannica's and Libertini's figures for armies and losses differ widely and are not used.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Baha al-Din ibn Shaddad's Life of Saladin, in the Palestine Pilgrims' Text Society translation of 1897, is an eyewitness account from Saladin's side; its editor's notes add place identifications and the Frankish order of march from the Itinerarium. The Itinerary of Richard I, the crusaders' own chronicle of the march, is read in the English translation published in Bohn's Chronicles of the Crusades (1848), which attributes it to Geoffrey de Vinsauf. Britannica's article and Christopher G. Libertini's EBSCO research starter give modern summaries.

perspectives.name: Richard I
perspectives.objective: Reach Jaffa with the army intact, as a base for an advance on Jerusalem.
perspectives.known: Saladin's army shadowed the march and attacked daily, trying to provoke the knights to charge.
perspectives.uncertainty: When the main Muslim army would come close enough for a charge to strike it, and whether his rearguard could hold until then.

perspectives.uncertainty: Whether the crusader knights could be provoked into charging at a moment of his choosing.
perspectives.constraints: His arrows made little impression on the mailed infantry, and the Turkoman reinforcements he expected had not yet arrived.

perspectives.logistics: Baha al-Din records rising barley prices in his camp and horses taken far to water.
perspectives.decision: He attacked the column on every side as it neared Arsuf and, when his army broke, rallied it around his squadron and drums.
perspectives.outcome: Defeat without destruction; he regrouped and offered battle again within days.

sources.publisher: German History in Documents and Images (trans. C. A. Macartney)

sources.title: Seven Years' War: The course of the Seven Years' War
Battle of Leuthen
Karl (Karl Alexander), Prinz von Lothringen
sources.publisher: Neue Deutsche Biographie (Rainer Egger), in German

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: The Seven Years' War arose from Austria's attempt to win back Silesia, which Frederick II had taken in the War of the Austrian Succession. In 1757 Frederick defeated the Austrians at Prague on 6 May but lost to Daun at Kolín on 18 June and evacuated Bohemia. Russian, Swedish, French and imperial armies threatened Prussia from several sides, and a Russian army defeated the Prussians at Gross-Jägerndorf on 30 August.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: While Frederick turned west and routed the French and imperial army at Rossbach on 5 November, the Austrians under Charles of Lorraine advanced in Silesia, defeated Brunswick-Bevern and took Schweidnitz on 11 November and Breslau; Britannica dates the fall of Breslau to 22 November, Egger's article to 24 November. Charles, Maria Theresa's brother-in-law, had lost to Frederick at Chotusitz in 1742, at Hohenfriedberg and Soor in 1745 and at Prague in 1757, but the empress kept him in command.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Frederick force-marched his army from Thuringia to restore the position in Silesia. On the eve of battle he told his officers that he would attack an enemy nearly twice as strong and entrenched on high ground, because if he did not, all was lost. The Austrians aimed to keep Silesia, the object of the war.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Beck notes that Frederick's generals knew the ground around Leuthen from Prussian peacetime manoeuvres, and that the main infantry marched toward the Austrian left under cover of the ground. The Austrians had left their fortified camp near Breslau to meet the Prussians near Leuthen; Frederick described them as entrenched on high ground.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Frederick commanded the Prussian army, which Beck describes as made up mostly of native Pomeranians and Brandenburgers, with high morale and mobile batteries of heavy guns. Charles of Lorraine commanded the much larger Austrian army. Britannica's and Beck's figures for the two armies differ and are not used.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: On 28 November Frederick wrote to his minister Finckenstein what GHDI calls a military testament, with orders for his burial and for the officers to swear allegiance to his brother should he fall. On 3 December, in an address reported in an 1802 publication, he told his officers that he would attack against all the rules of the art, offered to release any who wished to leave, and threatened to dismount any cavalry regiment that failed to charge and to take the colours from any infantry regiment that faltered.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: Frederick feigned an attack on the Austrian right. Convinced that the blow would fall there, the Austrian commander reinforced his right from the reserve. Meanwhile most of the Prussian infantry marched under cover toward the Austrian left and struck it about four miles south of the feint, supported by mobile batteries, forcing the Austrians to wheel from a north–south line to face south. An Austrian cavalry charge sent to relieve the infantry failed, and the Austrians fled in confusion; darkness on the short winter day prevented an immediate pursuit. Britannica summarises the rout as the work of an unexpected cavalry charge followed by an artillery bombardment.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Frederick chose to attack a larger army in position rather than wait, as his address says, and planned the feint and the march against the left flank; Beck calls his instructions of extraordinary clarity. Charles chose to leave the fortified camp near Breslau and meet the Prussians in the field and, taking the feint for the main attack, moved his reserves to the right.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: Reinforcing the right against the feint left the Austrian left to meet the main attack, and the failure of the cavalry charge sent to save the infantry turned the Austrian withdrawal into flight.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The Austrian army was routed, with losses, many of them prisoners, far above the Prussians'. The Prussians retook Breslau shortly afterwards, and Beck writes that Silesia was reconquered. Britannica calls Leuthen the greatest of Frederick's victories.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The empress, who had stood by Charles until then, relieved him of his command; Egger places his real importance in his government of the Austrian Netherlands. Britannica concludes that Frederick's handling of well-disciplined troops, together with the Russian general Apraksin's retreat, saved Prussia from a situation that had looked desperate after Kolín. The war went on until 1763.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Deception works when it fits the enemy's expectations: the feint drew the reserves to where they were not needed. Knowledge of the ground, here from peacetime manoeuvres, can make a concealed approach possible. Frederick's own words show the battle as a gamble taken because he judged that waiting meant ruin.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Frederick's address to his officers is known from a report published in 1802, and GHDI presents it as characteristic of his rhetoric, not as a verbatim record. GHDI's introduction dates the battle 4 December; Britannica and Egger give 5 December, which this study follows. Britannica attributes the rout to an unexpected cavalry charge followed by artillery, while Beck stresses the oblique attack, the terrain and the mobile batteries and calls Leuthen a textbook example of the oblique order. Figures for the armies and losses differ between Britannica and Beck and are not used. The older ADB article on Charles, printed on the same Deutsche Biographie page, judges him by no means a fortunate commander but a knowledgeable soldier; Egger's NDB article is more measured.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Frederick's testament and address, in C. A. Macartney's translation on German History in Documents and Images, give the king's view on the eve of battle. Britannica's history of the Seven Years' War places the battle in the campaign of 1757, and Hermann H. Beck's EBSCO research starter describes the manoeuvre. Rainer Egger's article in the Neue Deutsche Biographie, in German, gives the career of the Austrian commander. No Austrian account of the battle itself was read.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: The Ottoman Empire declared war on Russia on 16 August 1787, after Russia refused to return the Crimea, and on 9 February 1788 the Austrian envoy formally announced that Austria would fight at Russia's side. Beydilli lists the Ottoman setbacks that followed: the fall of Iași and Khotyn in September 1788 and the occupation of Moldavia, the loss of Ochakov (Özü) on 17 December 1788, with the killing of many of its inhabitants, and a defeat at Galați on 1 May 1789.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Selim III, who came to the throne on 7 April 1789, removed the grand vizier Koca Yusuf Pasha on 7 June and appointed Kethüdâ Hasan Pasha, who had won victories against Austria in this war. On the allied side Prince Josias of Saxe-Coburg commanded an Austrian corps and, Preradovich writes, fought in close cooperation with the Russians under Suvorov. Together they defeated an Ottoman army at Focșani, on 1 August 1789 according to Beydilli; the older ADB article gives 30 July.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: After Focșani the Ottoman army gathered its strength for a new offensive against Coburg's Austrian detachment. Suvorov aimed to join Coburg before the Ottomans could defeat it, and the allies then chose to attack rather than wait.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The battle was fought in Wallachia, across the river Rymna and toward the Rymnik (Râmnic). The allies crossed the Rymna to attack a camp at Tyrgo-Kukuli, then fortifications near the village of Bogsa, and finally the main Ottoman camp by the forest of Kryng-Malor. Beydilli places the Ottoman rout at the crossing of the Remnik and then on the bank of the Boza stream.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Suvorov brought a Russian detachment and on arrival took command of the whole allied force, according to the Presidential Library; Coburg commanded the Austrians. The Ottoman army was far larger. The Presidential Library names its commander as the grand vizier Yusuf Pasha, but Beydilli records that Yusuf had been removed as grand vizier in June and sent to command at Vidin. Numbers given for the armies are not used.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Hearing of the Ottoman advance, Suvorov's troops covered about 100 km in two and a half days and joined Coburg on 21 September (10 September in the Russian calendar). Suvorov's own account says Coburg wrote asking him to hurry, that he crossed the flooded Siret with grenadier, musketeer and light battalions formed in squares in two lines, with carabiniers, Cossacks and Arnauts, and that he then planned the march in two columns, leading the right himself while Coburg led the left. During the night before the battle the allied army moved off, fording the Rymna in silence.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: The Russians crossed the Rymna and attacked at 6 a.m. They silenced the Ottoman artillery, threw back the cavalry and after hard fighting took the camp at Tyrgo-Kukuli, driving its defenders toward the Rymnik. Meanwhile the Austrians repulsed a large cavalry attack that tried to split the allies. Suvorov writes that when Ottoman horsemen fell on one of his squares he moved another obliquely to catch them in crossfire, and that the Janissaries and Arab troops attacked with particular determination. Suvorov's troops took the fortifications near Bogsa and joined the Austrians. At 3 p.m. the allies attacked the main camp by the Kryng-Malor forest: the Austrians attacked it head-on in a long fight while Suvorov's troops outflanked the position and attacked with cavalry; in Suvorov's account he placed his carabiniers and hussars in the intervals between his squares and they leapt the unfinished entrenchment. The Ottoman army panicked and fled, and many drowned in the river.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Suvorov's decision to march at once to Coburg and take command of both armies, and the allied decision to attack a much larger enemy in its camps, shaped the battle. In the final attack the allies combined an Austrian frontal assault with a Russian flanking attack.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The repulse of the Ottoman cavalry that tried to split the allies let the two armies join. The Russian outflanking of the main camp, together with the Austrian frontal attack, broke the Ottoman army, and the river behind it turned the retreat into a disaster.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The Ottoman army was routed with heavy losses of men, transport and artillery, while allied losses were light. Suvorov writes that the grand vizier, who had stood by the forest during the battle, could not halt his fleeing troops, retreated to Brăila and had the bridge over the Buzău raised behind him. Beydilli counts the defeat at the Remnik and the rout on the Boza among the disasters of 1789.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Catherine II made Suvorov a count with the title Rymniksky, and Joseph II made him a count of the Holy Roman Empire. Coburg was made field marshal and entered Bucharest in triumph. Beydilli writes that the defeats of 1789 and the loss of fortresses that followed showed a crisis that changes of grand vizier could not mend: when Cezayirli Hasan Pasha became grand vizier in December 1789, the army's leaders were hoping for peace.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Allied armies can act as one when a single plan coordinates them: speed of march and a shared attack let two smaller forces defeat a larger one before it could deal with them separately.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The national traditions tell the battle differently. The Russian Presidential Library gives Suvorov command of the whole allied force and the decisive flanking attack; Preradovich's NDB article calls the victory at Martinești on the Rimnik Coburg's, for which he was made field marshal; Beydilli's Ottoman account counts it among a series of disasters. Suvorov's own account, written in 1790 to support the grant of his title, is more measured about command than the Presidential Library: it has each general lead a column and Suvorov ask Coburg to press his squares forward. It is also the source of the Russian figures, which are not used. The Ottoman commander is unclear in the sources read: the Presidential Library names the grand vizier Yusuf Pasha and Suvorov speaks only of the grand vizier, while Beydilli has Yusuf replaced as grand vizier in June 1789 by Kethüdâ Hasan Pasha. The Presidential Library's casualty estimates range widely and are not used. Russian dates of the time run eleven days behind the Western calendar.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: The Russian Presidential Library's page, which draws on nineteenth-century Russian publications including Suvorov's own report, gives the course of the battle. Suvorov's autobiography of 1790, in Russian on Wikisource, gives his own account of the march and the battle. Kemal Beydilli's article on Koca Yusuf Pasha in the TDV İslâm Ansiklopedisi, in Turkish, gives the Ottoman chronology of the war. Nikolaus von Preradovich's NDB article on Coburg, in German, gives the Austrian view; the same page holds August Beck's older ADB article. No Ottoman account of the battle itself was read.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: Vicksburg, on bluffs above the Mississippi, was fortified by the Confederate army under John C. Pemberton, which, the Park Service writes, had more than a year to build earthworks and mount more than 170 cannon. Grant writes that its fall would give the Union the whole river and divide the Confederacy. From December 1862 his attempts to reach the city, from the north and through the bayous west of the river, failed to bring him onto dry ground on the enemy's side.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Grant writes that the elections of 1862 had gone against the prosecution of the war, voluntary enlistment had nearly ceased and the draft was resisted, so that a defeat or a backward movement would have made the draft impossible to enforce. A forward movement to a decisive victory, he concluded, was necessary. The Mississippi Encyclopedia gives the Confederate side: Jefferson Davis, himself a Mississippian, thought the town symbolically important and knew that the railroad running east from it to Jackson was a vital lifeline; after the defeat at Corinth he sent John C. Pemberton, a Pennsylvania-born general, to command there.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Grant first planned to get below Vicksburg, join Nathaniel Banks against Port Hudson and use New Orleans as a base. When Banks wrote that he could not be at Port Hudson for ten days, Grant judged the time worth more than the reinforcements and pushed into the interior. Pemberton's aim was to hold Vicksburg; Joseph E. Johnston, gathering forces to the east, aimed to raise the siege. Davis writes that Pemberton had laid in supplies for an ordinary siege and, knowing how much the government valued the city, counted on a relieving army to break any investment; on 9 May Johnston was ordered to Mississippi to take chief command, with reinforcements from Bragg and Beauregard.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Grant calls the country between the river and the Big Black admirable for defence but difficult for an offensive campaign. The landing at Bruinsburg lay two miles from high ground. Vicksburg stands on ridges of deep yellow clay of great tenacity, and its civilians dug shelters into the hillsides; the Park Service describes caves of different sizes and shapes, some T- or Y-shaped, damp and poorly ventilated, which a direct mortar hit could collapse.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Grant commanded the Army of the Tennessee, with corps under McClernand, McPherson and Sherman, supported by Admiral Porter's gunboats; without the navy, Grant writes, the campaign could not have been made in the way it was with any number of men. Pemberton commanded at Vicksburg; Johnston commanded the forces gathering in Grant's rear. Grant gives strengths for both sides at several points; the figures are his and are not used.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: After an attack on Grand Gulf, Grant's army crossed the river below Vicksburg, and on the morning of 30 April McClernand's corps and one division of McPherson's landed at Bruinsburg. Grant writes that he felt a relief scarcely ever equalled: he was in the enemy's country with the river and Vicksburg between him and his base of supplies, but on dry ground on the same side as the enemy.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: Marching inland on five days' rations and no forage, Grant's army fought and won at Port Gibson, Raymond, Jackson, Champion's Hill and the Big Black, took the state capital and destroyed its military works, and drove Pemberton's army into Vicksburg. At Champion Hill on 16 May, the Mississippi Encyclopedia notes, the hill changed hands three times before Pemberton's three divisions were driven off; Loring's division was cut off and marched away east, and the rest fell back into the city. On 19 May, twenty days after the crossing, the city was invested and an assault failed; a larger assault on 22 May also failed, and from 23 May Grant laid regular siege, bringing up supplies by roads from the Yazoo River. On 7 June Confederate troops attacked the Union depot at Milliken's Bend, where they met untested United States Colored Troops. On 3 July Pemberton opened correspondence; after a meeting with Grant he accepted terms, and on 4 July the garrison marched out, stacked arms and was paroled.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Grant pushed inland without waiting for Banks and, after the failed assault of 22 May, chose to out-camp the enemy rather than lose more men. On the Confederate side, Davis's account turns on Johnston: arriving at Jackson on 13 May, he telegraphed that he was too late, halted there instead of joining Pemberton, and ordered him to come up in the rear of Sherman's force. Pemberton, who doubted the move, put it to a council of war, which split between Johnston's plan and a march against Grant's supply line; he set out against the supply line, turned back on a fresh order from Johnston, and was caught and beaten at Champion Hill. After the Big Black, Johnston wrote that if Vicksburg was invested it must ultimately surrender and that the army should evacuate it; Pemberton's council judged unanimously that the army could not be withdrawn in a state to be of further service, and he resolved to hold what he called the most important point in the Confederacy. At the surrender Grant first demanded unconditional surrender, then, against the almost unanimous judgment of his council, offered terms that let the garrison sign paroles and march out. Under the exchange cartel, he explains, prisoners had to be exchanged or paroled, and shipping more than thirty thousand men north would have cost great expense only for them to be paroled at the end. Pemberton wrote in his report that he chose 4 July expecting better terms from the Union's national vanity; Grant thought he chose it to avoid an assault he knew would succeed.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The crossing at Bruinsburg and the rapid march inland let Grant meet the Confederate forces separately, before they could combine, and the capture of Jackson cut Vicksburg off from the east. Once the navy held the river and the army closed the land side, the garrison was limited to what it had.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: After 47 days of siege the Confederate army surrendered on 4 July with its arms and cannon. Pemberton's report, quoted by Davis, says he made terms not because his men were starved out but because they were overpowered by numbers and worn down by forty-seven days and nights in the trenches without relief, and that his division commanders judged them unable to cut their way out. Grant writes that the two armies began to fraternise as soon as his men entered the lines, his soldiers giving bread from their haversacks to men they had been starving out. The fall of Vicksburg brought the surrender of Port Hudson, and with it the whole Mississippi.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Grant writes that the capture, together with Gettysburg, gave new spirit to the North, that the Union now held the whole river, and that the Confederacy was cut in two. Sherman then drove Johnston from Jackson. Grant ordered food and medicine for destitute families along the army's route, whose resources had been taken for its supply. After the siege, the Park Service notes, residents left the caves to erode.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Speed can substitute for a secure supply line when the enemy's forces are divided. Army and navy together made the campaign possible; Grant judged it impossible without the navy.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Grant's memoirs, written twenty years later, are the victor's account; his remark that Providence seemed to direct the campaign and his figures for both sides are his. He prints Pemberton's own explanation of the 4 July surrender beside his contrary reading. Halleck feared that paroling the garrison would put the men back in the Confederate ranks; Grant notes they had already been delivered to the Confederate exchange commissioner. The Confederate accounts are partisan in their own way: Davis's memoir, published in 1881, defends Pemberton and his own administration and lays the confusion before Champion Hill on Johnston's decision to stay at Jackson, and the Mississippi Encyclopedia agrees that Johnston's relieving army did not move until it was too late. Whether hunger forced the surrender is disputed: Pemberton denied it, while Grant speaks of a garrison being starved out. The civilian experience of the siege is barely present in Grant's account.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Grant's Personal Memoirs, on Project Gutenberg, give the commander's narrative and quote Pemberton's report. The National Park Service's pages on the siege and on cave life, from Vicksburg National Military Park, give the course of the siege and the civilians' shelters. Jefferson Davis's Rise and Fall of the Confederate Government gives the Confederate president's account of the campaign, with Johnston's and Pemberton's dispatches and Pemberton's report. Michael B. Ballard's overview of the Civil War and Ben Wynne's entry on Champion Hill in the Mississippi Encyclopedia give the Confederate command, Davis's view of Vicksburg and the decisive battle inland.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: In spring 1864 Grant planned movements in several theatres at once. His orders to Sherman, which Sherman prints, were to move against Johnston's army, break it up, get into the interior of the enemy's country as far as he could and inflict all the damage he could against its war resources, leaving the plan to Sherman. Atlanta, a manufacturing centre and rail hub, was at stake; Johnston's Army of Tennessee stood at Dalton.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: A presidential election was due in November 1864, with Lincoln against General McClellan, nominated by the Democrats. Sherman records Lincoln telling him later that he had been in doubt that summer, with Grant seemingly checkmated before Richmond and Petersburg and Sherman's army apparently stopped before an impassable barrier.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Sherman aimed at Johnston's army and the resources behind it, and in practice manoeuvred to threaten the railroad behind each Confederate position. Johnston, the Battlefield Trust writes, planned to hold strong defensive ground and wait for an attack. In his own Narrative Johnston explains why: at Dalton a defeat would have been disastrous with Atlanta far behind, while a victory could not have been decisive with Chattanooga close behind Sherman; fighting from entrenchments, he hoped to wear down the larger Union army and then fight on equal ground beyond the Chattahoochee, with Atlanta as a refuge. Hood, who replaced him, preferred what he called the school of Lee and Jackson and condemned Johnston's policy as a timid defensive.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The campaign ran south from Dalton along the Western & Atlantic Railroad, across ridges and rivers: Rocky Face Ridge, the Oostanaula and Etowah, the hills about Kennesaw and the Chattahoochee. Atlanta depended on railroads. Hood writes that the road to Augusta was lost before he took command, that the West Point road lay within the enemy's reach, and that the Macon railroad was his remaining line of supply.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Sherman commanded three armies, under George H. Thomas, James B. McPherson and John M. Schofield. Johnston commanded the Confederate Army of Tennessee until July, when Jefferson Davis replaced him with John B. Hood; Hood writes that the order reached him about 11 p.m. on 17 July. Hood calls himself comparatively a stranger to the army, and writes that the senior corps commander felt supplanted. The strengths the Battlefield Trust gives are not used.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: From early May, Thomas and Schofield demonstrated against the Confederate lines while McPherson moved round Johnston's left to threaten the railroad behind him, a pattern repeated through the campaign. Johnston left Rocky Face Ridge on 12 May.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: After sharp fighting at Resaca on 14–15 May, McPherson crossed the Oostanaula and Johnston fell back; a Confederate attack at Cassville on 19 May came to nothing, and inconclusive fighting followed around Dallas, New Hope Church and Pickett's Mill. On 27 June Sherman assaulted the fortified lines at Kennesaw Mountain; by 11.30 the assault had failed. Flanked again, Johnston fell back across the Chattahoochee in early July. Hood attacked at Peachtree Creek on 20 July and on 22 July sent Hardee's corps on a flank attack in which McPherson was killed, but the Confederates were repulsed. Sherman moved by his right to cut the Macon railroad, with fighting at Ezra Church and Utoy Creek. On 31 August Union troops reached the railroad near Jonesboro, and on 1 September Davis's corps carried the Confederate works there. Hood evacuated Atlanta that night, and the city surrendered on 2 September.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Sherman avoided frontal attack except at Kennesaw, where, after consulting Thomas, McPherson and Schofield, he judged that they could not stretch further and that there was no alternative but to attack fortified lines, a thing carefully avoided until then. Johnston writes that he repeatedly urged the government, directly and through General Bragg, to send Forrest's cavalry from Mississippi against the railroad that supplied Sherman, since his own cavalry was too weak and needed at the front, and that the troops meant for it were each time diverted. Davis's decision to replace Johnston with Hood brought a change to the offensive, and Hood's attacks at Peachtree Creek and on 22 July followed the doctrine he preferred.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: Hood's failure to break Sherman's armies in the July battles left him defending a city whose supply depended on railroads Sherman could reach. Once Union troops held the Macon railroad near Jonesboro, Atlanta could not be held.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Hood abandoned Atlanta on the night of 1 September, and the city surrendered to Federal forces the next morning. The news that Atlanta was “ours, and fairly won” spread across the North. Losses over the four months were heavy on both sides; the figures are not used.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The Battlefield Trust judges that the capture all but assured Lincoln's re-election two months later and set up the March to the Sea. In September Sherman ordered Atlanta's civilians to leave, south or north. Hood protested, calling the measure unprecedented and an act of studied and ingenious cruelty; Sherman replied that Confederate commanders had themselves removed families and had fought so close to towns that shots fell among houses. In his memoirs Sherman gives his real reasons: he wanted the houses for military use and shorter lines, and wanted to be free of feeding and policing a civilian population.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Manoeuvre against an enemy's communications can win ground without costly assaults; Sherman's one large frontal attack, at Kennesaw, failed. Changing a commander to change a strategy carries risk when the army has been trained to the old one.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Whether Johnston's retreats or Hood's attacks better served the Confederacy is a long-running dispute, and all three memoirs read here take sides. Johnston's Narrative answers the charges made after his removal: that he disregarded the president's instructions, would not fight and refused to defend Atlanta. He says Davis gave him no instruction beyond a warning not to fight with the Chattahoochee close behind, contrasts the government's patience with other retreating generals, and disputes Hood's figures for his losses. Hood's, written after Sherman's, is largely a reply to Johnston: he blames Johnston's policy for an army unfit for pitched battle and accuses him of leaving without giving the promised counsel. Sherman disputes Johnston's estimate of Union losses at Kennesaw, and Johnston's own estimates of Union losses are not used. Sherman's justification for expelling Atlanta's civilians and Hood's protest are both advocacy. The Battlefield Trust's article is unsigned and cites no sources.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: The American Battlefield Trust's article gives the course of the campaign. Sherman's Memoirs, on Project Gutenberg, give his orders, the Kennesaw assault, the fall of the city and his reasons for removing its people. Hood's Advance and Retreat (1880) and Johnston's Narrative of Military Operations (1874), both on the Internet Archive, give the two Confederate commanders' opposing views, including Hood's September correspondence with Sherman and Johnston's defence of his strategy.

perspectives.name: William T. Sherman
perspectives.objective: Break up Johnston's army and reach Atlanta and the South's war resources.

sources.title: Battle of Adwa
Battle of Adowa
Emperor Menelik II of Ethiopia and the Battle of Adwa: A Pictorial History
Baratieri, Oreste
sources.publisher: Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani (Mariano Gabriele), in Italian

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: After Emperor Yohannes IV died in 1889, Sahle Mariam of Shewa, whom Italy had supplied with weapons, ammunition and money, secured the imperial title as Menelik II. The Treaty of Wichale (Ucciali) of 2 May 1889 promised an Italian loan and recognised Italy's claim to Eritrea. Menelik read its Article XVII as allowing Ethiopia to use the Italian government in dealing with other powers; the Italian premier Francesco Crispi read it as requiring that, which implied a protectorate. Menelik repudiated the article in 1890 and the whole treaty in 1893.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Oreste Baratieri, governor of Eritrea from 1892, hoped to enlarge the colony. Gabriele records his victories over Ras Mangasha at Coatit and Senafe in January 1895, the occupation of Adigrat, Mekele, Adwa and Axum, and the Italian government's refusal of reinforcements, divided between Crispi's African ambitions and Sonnino's economies. Menelik's general mobilisation followed. In December 1895 a force under Major Toselli was destroyed at Amba Alagi by troops led by Ras Makonnen, and on 20 January 1896 the besieged fort at Mekele ended its resistance.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Menelik prepared to resist any Italian attempt to impose dominion by force. Crispi wanted a quick success of prestige, while Baratieri, by Gabriele's account, by then wanted a purely defensive war. Both armies, Britannica says, were short of supplies, and each waited for the other to strike first.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The armies faced each other near Adwa in Tigray, in north-central Ethiopia. The Italians lacked reliable maps, and Britannica describes their columns as unable to find their way across the terrain. Gabriele describes the retreat as especially costly in the valley of Iehà, where Ethiopian cavalry charged the withdrawing troops.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Menelik's army, well armed with modern weapons, was far larger than Baratieri's; Menelik played down its size with false reports and rumours of discord among his forces. The Library of Congress notes that Taytu, his consort, warned him against Italian emissaries and controlled the enemy's water sources. Baratieri's force comprised Italian brigades and African askari, with columns under Albertone, Arimondi, Dabormida and Ellena. The figures the sources give are not used.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Under pressure from Rome, Baratieri met his generals. Britannica says he at first seemed to favour retreat but was persuaded to fight; Gabriele places the council at Saurià on 28 February, where Arimondi's rash offensive view prevailed over Baratieri's opposition, and notes that Baratieri's order of 29 February gave no clear directions for what to do once the first objectives were reached or if a retreat became necessary. On the night of 29 February the Italians advanced on Adwa in separate columns, aiming to surprise the Ethiopians.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: On 1 March the columns lost touch with each other and fought almost in isolation. Albertone's brigade was destroyed first, although its artillery at one point caused some disorder among the Ethiopians. Ethiopian forces surrounded the isolated columns and fought them at close quarters, cancelling the Italian advantage in long-range weapons. Small Italian counter-attacks held for a time, but as Ellena's and Arimondi's brigades gave way the retreat became confused. Dabormida's column on the right, which had kept attacking on its own, was surrounded; Dabormida was killed, and his troops broke out and retreated.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Menelik concealed his strength and waited while his army could still be fed. Baratieri, pressed by Rome and with his successor already designated, accepted an offensive he opposed. His plan to surprise the Ethiopians with converging columns failed when the columns lost coordination.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The separation of the Italian columns, beginning with Albertone's, let the Ethiopians defeat them one after another before they could support each other.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The Italian army was routed, losing very heavily in killed and prisoners among both Italian and askari troops. Ethiopian losses were also heavy, though a small share of the whole army. The sources' figures differ and are not used.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: In Italy the defeat brought Crispi's resignation. Baratieri was tried by a military tribunal at Asmara for omissions, negligence and abandoning his command, was acquitted, and left the army. The Treaty of Addis Ababa of October 1896 abrogated Wichale, and Italy abandoned its claim to a protectorate. Britannica writes that the victory gave Menelik credibility with the European powers and a period of peace, and calls it the first crushing defeat of a European power by African forces in the colonial era. Through Coptic mediation, the Library of Congress notes, Italian prisoners were released from November 1896.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Concentration defeats dispersion: separated columns advancing over unfamiliar ground can be destroyed one by one. Political pressure from a distant capital can push a commander into a battle he doubts.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The sources disagree on the run-up: Britannica dates Crispi's goading telegram to 28 February and the council to the next day, while Gabriele dates the telegram, which spoke of military consumption, to 25 February and the council to 28 February. Italian writers long argued over Baratieri's responsibility; Gabriele's bibliography includes works written in his defence and for his rehabilitation, and the 1896 tribunal acquitted him. Casualty estimates vary between sources and are not used. The Ethiopian paintings held by the Library of Congress, such as Shibru Nuru's of 1975 with St George above the battle, present it as a national and religious triumph, while European images of the time range from caricature to respectful trade cards.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Britannica gives the narrative and the outcome; Shumet Sishagne's EBSCO research starter gives the conduct of the battle on the Ethiopian side; Fentahun Tiruneh's Library of Congress article presents the Ethiopian visual tradition and the aftermath; Mariano Gabriele's article in the Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, in Italian, gives the Italian command and the battle by brigades. No Ethiopian chronicle and neither Baratieri's memoirs nor the Italian official history were read.

Jadunath Sarkar, Shivaji and His Times
Shivaji
James Grant Duff, A History of the Mahrattas, vol. 1 (London, 1826)

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: Shivaji's father, Shahji, served the sultan of Bijapur. From about 1655, Britannica writes, Shivaji began to seize the weaker Bijapur outposts in the Western Ghats. Sarkar describes his conquest of Javli and his enlistment of Pathan mercenaries from the disbanded soldiery of Bijapur.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Bijapur's resources had been crippled by war with the Mughals and, Sarkar writes, by a regency under the Dowager Queen. The command against Shivaji went begging at court until Afzal Khan, a general of the first rank, accepted it; the Sabhasad Bakhar has him boast that he would bring Shivaji back a prisoner without once dismounting from his horse.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Afzal Khan, Sarkar writes, did not want an open contest of force in the hills; he planned to win over the Maval chiefs and, on the Dowager Queen's instructions, to capture or kill Shivaji by pretending friendship. Through his envoy he offered to secure Shivaji's pardon and the confirmation of his forts. Grant Duff adds that Afzal had once governed the Wai district and so knew how hard the country would be to penetrate. Shivaji's aim was to keep his independence: capitulation, Sarkar writes, would have ended his hopes for ever.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Pratapgad stands in the forested Western Ghats near the Mahabaleshwar plateau. Afzal Khan descended by the Radtondi pass and camped at Par, a mile below the fort, his men scattered in the valley near the pools at the source of the Koyna. The meeting place was an eminence below the fort, reached by a forest path.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Afzal Khan led regular Bijapur forces with artillery, elephants and transport; Khandoji Khopde, a Maval deshmukh who had promised to arrest Shivaji in return for a coveted office, led his vanguard. Shivaji's forces were mainly Mavle infantry, with armies under Netaji Palkar above the Ghats and Moro Pant from the Konkan. Figures for Afzal's army differ between contemporary and later Maratha accounts, and none is used.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: At a first council Shivaji's officers urged peace; after a night of reflection, and a vision of the goddess Bhavani that the Bakhar records, he resolved to fight and left instructions for the government should he die. Envoys passed between the camps, and Shivaji's agent Gopinath (Pantaji) learnt by bribes that Afzal's officers expected Shivaji to be seized at the meeting; he urged Shivaji to strike first. Shivaji feigned fear and asked the Khan to come to Javli, where a path was cut and food laid ready for his army. He posted men in ambush along the forest path to the pavilion and brought Netaji Palkar and Moro Pant within reach, to attack on the signal of a gun from the fort.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: Afzal Khan left his escort of musketeers behind and came up in a palanquin with two soldiers, the swordsman Sayyid Banda and the envoys; at Shivaji's request Sayyid Banda was sent away. Shivaji came with two armed companions, wearing armour under his clothes, with steel claws in his left hand and a dagger. As they embraced, both the Bakhar and Sarkar say, the Khan held Shivaji's head under his arm and struck at his side with a dagger, which the armour turned; Shivaji tore him open with the claws and stabbed him. Sambhaji Kavji cut down the bearers and beheaded the Khan, and Jiv Mahala struck down Sayyid Banda. A gun was fired from the fort, and the waiting Maratha forces fell on the camp from four sides; Sarkar describes about three hours of desperate fighting by groups without a common plan.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Shivaji chose to fight rather than submit, against his council's advice, and to meet the Khan only on his own ground, near his fort and his concealed forces. Afzal Khan agreed to come to Javli and, at Gopinath's urging, left his escort behind.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The death of the commander at the meeting left an army in unknown, forested country without leadership. Sarkar argues that Afzal, expecting Shivaji's death to end his power at once, had not kept his troops ready and did not know that two Maratha armies were close by.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The Bijapur army was destroyed or dispersed, and its artillery, treasure, elephants, horses and baggage were taken. Those who begged for quarter were spared, and women, children, Brahmans and camp-followers released; Afzal Khan's eldest son, Fazl Khan, escaped through the forest. Shivaji enlisted the sons of his fallen men, pensioned their widows at half pay and rewarded the wounded.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Overnight, Britannica writes, Shivaji became a formidable warlord with the horses, guns and ammunition of the Bijapur army. Sarkar dates the victory to 10 November 1659 and describes the Marathas pouring into South Konkan and the Kolhapur country, taking Panhala and defeating another Bijapur army by February 1660, before Siddi Jauhar besieged Shivaji in Panhala in March. Among the Marathas the event became the most celebrated of Shivaji's life, sung in ballads.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: A parley between enemies is dangerous ground: here each side prepared for treachery by the other. Forces hidden in country they know let a smaller army exploit the moment when an enemy's command is removed.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Who intended treachery is the central dispute. Britannica writes that Shivaji lured the Khan to the meeting with submissive appeals and killed him. Sarkar, citing a contemporary English factory letter from Rajapur that Bijapur told the Khan to take Shivaji by pretending friendship, concludes that Afzal struck first and calls Shivaji's act, after Burke, a preventive murder. Sarkar notes that Khafi Khan, a later Mughal historian, says both men came unarmed, and Sen's notes say that Grant Duff's account follows Khafi Khan. Grant Duff, read directly, cites Maratha and Persian manuscripts and English records: he has Shivaji win over the Khan's Brahmin envoy, Pantoji Gopinath, with an appeal to religion and the promise of a village, plan the meeting as an ambush, and strike first during the embrace with the steel claws, while the Khan cried treachery. Writing as a former East India Company officer in 1826, he speaks of the vanity of a Mahomedan noble and of the treacherous Mahratta, and his version is the one that Sarkar's conclusion contradicts. The Sabhasad Bakhar, which Sarkar dates to 1694, is a devotional narrative with prophecies and a vision of the goddess, and Sarkar cites reasons to doubt its stories of Afzal's desecration of temples as later popular inventions. Sen's note dates Afzal's death to September 1659; Sarkar gives 10 November, which this study follows.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: The Sabhasad Bakhar, in Surendranath Sen's translation of 1920, is the Maratha court account. Jadunath Sarkar's Shivaji and His Times weighs it against Persian histories and the English factory records, with an appendix on the evidence for the affair. James Grant Duff's History of the Mahrattas (1826), on the Internet Archive, gives an early British narrative, in which Shivaji is the aggressor. Ranjit Ramchandra Desai's Britannica biography gives the modern summary. No Bijapur chronicle was read except as Sarkar reports it.

金史 卷九十三 (Jin Shi, chapter 93): biographies of Dujie Sizhong and Wanyan Chengyu
元史 卷一百十九 (Yuan Shi, chapter 119): biography of Muqali
Genghis Khan: Rise to power

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: In 1206 an assembly by the Onon proclaimed Temüjin Chinggis Khan, and his new state was organised above all for war. China was his main goal; Britannica writes that he first secured his western flank with a hard campaign against the Tangut kingdom of Xixia, then fell on the Jin empire of northern China in 1211. The Yuan Shi records that Jin defectors told him their ruler had killed members of his own family and lived in growing debauchery, and has Chinggis reply that his campaign now had a just cause.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: The Jin had long played the steppe peoples against each other, and Britannica notes that they once rewarded Temüjin with a minor title for attacking the Tatars. The Jin Shi records that in the Dading reign a line of northwestern frontier posts nearly 600 li long had been built, and that Dujie Sizhong later strengthened its walls and moats. In the third year of Da'an Dujie Sizhong and the councillor Wanyan Chengyu were sent to hold the frontier.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Chinggis aimed at the Jin heartland: the Secret History has him take Fuzhou, the Jin's northernmost outpost, and send vanguards on toward the passes before the capital, Zhongdu. The Jin aimed to hold the frontier and the passes. Britannica notes that Chinggis at first meant to turn the fields of northern China into pasture, until an adviser who had served the Jin explained the value of peasants and craftsmen as producers of taxable goods.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The fighting moved from the frontier near Fuzhou through the uplands of Yehuling (Wild Fox Ridge), where the Yuan Shi says the Jin drew up, south to Xuanping, the Huihe stream and Xuande, and on toward the Juyong Pass before Zhongdu. The Jin Shi has the local strongmen of Xuanping say that they knew the winding streams and gullies. The Secret History describes valleys and mountains filling with pursuing Jin troops.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Chinggis led the Mongol army, with Muqali, Jebe and Güyigünek among his commanders. Wanyan Chengyu commanded the Jin field army after Dujie Sizhong's dismissal; the Secret History names among the Jin forces the élite Jüyin troops of the Qara Kitat and the Jurchen. The Yuan Shi says the Jin army was called four hundred thousand strong; the figure is not used here.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Dujie Sizhong and Chengyu were repairing the fort at Wushabu without taking precautions when the Mongol vanguard arrived suddenly and took the Wuyue camp; Dujie Sizhong could not hold it and fell back. The court blamed him alone, dismissed him and gave Chengyu the command.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: In the eighth month the Mongol army reached Yehuling. The Jin Shi says that Chengyu lost heart and fell back to Xuanping without fighting, refused the local levies offered to him as a vanguard and asked only for a side road to Xuande, and that the local strongmen scoffed that he knew only how to run. That night he marched south; the Mongols followed, and the next day his army broke at Huihechuan and he escaped alone into Xuande. The Yuan Shi tells the battle from the Mongol side: the Jin drew up north of Yehuling, Muqali led picked men in a charge, Chinggis sent the whole army forward, and the pursuit reached the Hui river. In the Secret History, after the army has crossed the pass it calls Hünegen Daba'an, Jebe feigns a retreat at the Chabchiyal pass to draw the Jin out, turns on them, and the main army crushes the Jin élite troops.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: The Jin Shi explains the defeat by Chengyu's decisions to avoid battle, to retreat by night and to refuse the local levies. On the Mongol side the Yuan Shi credits Muqali's judgment that, being fewer, they must fight to the death, and Chinggis's order for a general advance behind his charge.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The night retreat turned an army that had not been beaten in the field into a column pursued from behind, and the collapse at Huihechuan followed. The Jin Shi's verdict is that the commanders' spirit was broken, quoting the saying that the first drum rouses courage, the second weakens it and the third exhausts it.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The Jin field army was destroyed, and Chengyu barely escaped. Mongol raiders entered the Juyong Pass, and martial law was proclaimed in Zhongdu. Prince Weishao, the Jin ruler, punished Chengyu only by removing him from office.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The Jin Shi records that observers held that the fall of the Jin was decided in this battle. In the Secret History the Jin official Ongging Cingsang later advises the Golden Khan, during the siege of Zhongdu, that the élite troops have been destroyed and the Chabchiyal pass lost, and that it is better to submit and send a princess and gifts. Britannica dates that settlement to 1214; operations resumed in 1215, Beijing was taken, and the subjugation of northern China passed to Muqali.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: An army's will can be broken before it is beaten: the Jin historians blamed a commander who retreated without fighting and ignored the local knowledge offered to him. A retreat in contact with a mobile enemy can be more dangerous than battle.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The three accounts come from different sides and differ in detail. The Jin Shi dates the battle to the eighth month of the third year of Da'an, the Secret History places the campaign in the Year of the Sheep (1211), but the Yuan Shi's biography of Muqali puts the battle at Yehuling in the year renshen (1212) and the attack on the Juyong Pass in 1213. The Secret History does not name Yehuling; it describes the crossing of a pass it calls Hünegen Daba'an and fighting at the Chabchiyal pass, and the sources read do not say how these places correspond to those named in the Chinese histories. The Yuan Shi's figure for the Jin army and its hundred li of corpses are not used, and Muqali's words are reported speech. The Jin Shi's portrait of Chengyu as a coward is a historian's explanation of a dynasty's fall.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: The Secret History of the Mongols, in Igor de Rachewiltz's open-access translation, gives the Mongol narrative of the campaign. The Jin Shi's biographies of Dujie Sizhong and Wanyan Chengyu, and the Yuan Shi's biography of Muqali, both read in Chinese on Wikisource, give the Jin and the Mongol-Yuan accounts of the battle. Charles R. Bawden's Britannica biography of Genghis Khan gives the wider context. No modern study of the battle itself was read.
